title: CA Final Direct Taxes - Profits and Gains of Business or Profession (PGBP) Complete Conceptual Mastery
description: Comprehensive conceptual clarity MCQ set covering every substantive condition, exception, distinction, consequence, and landmark case law across all provisions of PGBP.

questions.question: An assessee carried on an active trading business during April and May of the previous year and permanently shut down operations on 31st May. Under which head and on what basis are the profits earned during those two months assessed?
options: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession, because the business was carried on at any time during the previous year
Income from Other Sources, because the business was not in active existence on the last day of the previous year
Capital Gains, as discontinuance of business converts operational profits into realization of capital assets
Exempt from income-tax, because business profits are taxable only if operations continue for the full financial year
questions.explanation: Under the charging section for PGBP, profits and gains of any business or profession carried on by the assessee at any time during the previous year are chargeable to tax under PGBP. Continuous operation throughout the entire previous year is not required.

questions.question: A manufacturer receives Duty Entitlement Pass Book (DEPB) credit and Cash Compensatory Support upon completing overseas export shipments. What is the correct income-tax character and head of income for these receipts?
options: Capital receipts reducing the actual cost of plant and machinery
Specific statutory business receipts taxable under Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
Casual non-recurring income taxable under Income from Other Sources
Exempt subsidies granted to promote national foreign trade
questions.explanation: Profit on sale of import entitlement licences, cash compensatory support, duty drawback, DEPB, and DFRC are specific statutory inclusions under the charging section chargeable under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession'.

questions.question: A corporate employer receives ₹50,00,000 upon maturity of a Keyman Insurance Policy taken on the life of its chief operating officer, including ₹8,00,000 allocated as bonus. How is this total maturity payout taxed?
options: Exempt from income-tax as a maturity receipt from a life insurance policy
Taxable under Capital Gains after deducting total insurance premiums paid over the policy tenure
Taxable as business income under Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
Taxable under Income from Other Sources as an ex-gratia windfall
questions.explanation: Any sum received under a Keyman insurance policy, including the sum allocated by way of bonus on such policy, is specifically chargeable to income-tax under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession'.

questions.question: An architect receives a luxury sedan from a real estate developer as a performance reward for designing an award-winning commercial complex. The architect claims the car is a tax-free personal gift in kind. What is the correct tax treatment?
options: Non-taxable, because movable assets received without monetary conversion cannot constitute income
Taxable under Income from Other Sources only if the architect sells the car within the same previous year
Treated as an adjustment to personal capital with zero income-tax liability
Taxable under PGBP at fair market value, as the value of any benefit or perquisite arising from business or profession is chargeable whether convertible into money or not
questions.explanation: The value of any benefit or perquisite arising from business or the exercise of a profession is taxable under PGBP, irrespective of whether it is convertible into money or not, and whether received in cash or in kind.

questions.question: A partnership firm pays ₹6,00,000 as salary to its working partner. In the assessment of the firm, ₹2,00,000 is disallowed being in excess of the statutory book profit limit. What amount is taxable in the hands of the partner under PGBP?
options: ₹4,00,000, because partner remuneration is taxable under PGBP only to the extent it was allowed as a deduction to the firm
₹6,00,000, because the partner actually received the full salary from the partnership firm
Nil, because mutual transactions between partners and their firm are completely exempt from tax
₹2,00,000, being the amount disallowed in the assessment of the partnership firm
questions.explanation: Under the interaction principle between partner and firm taxation, salary, interest, bonus, or commission received by a partner is taxable under PGBP only to the extent it has been allowed as a deduction in the computation of income of the firm. The disallowed portion (₹2,00,000) is not taxable in the partner's hands.

questions.question: A firm credits interest on capital of ₹1,80,000 (calculated at 18% simple interest per annum) to a partner's capital account. If the firm is allowed deduction only at 12% per annum (₹1,20,000), how is the partner assessed?
options: ₹1,80,000 is taxable under Income from Other Sources
₹1,20,000 is taxable under PGBP, and the excess ₹60,000 disallowed to the firm is not taxable in the partner's hands
₹1,80,000 is taxable under PGBP with a tax credit for the firm's disallowance
The entire ₹1,80,000 is exempt from tax in the hands of the partner
questions.explanation: Interest received by a partner from a firm is taxable under PGBP only to the extent allowed as a deduction to the firm (i.e. at 12% p.a., equaling ₹1,20,000). The excess interest disallowed to the firm is not taxable in the partner's hands.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical scientist enters into a restrictive covenant agreeing not to share proprietary chemical synthesis know-how with any competitor for a period of 5 years and receives ₹40,00,000. How is this receipt treated?
options: Exempt capital receipt representing the sterilisation of personal intellectual capacity
Taxable under Capital Gains as consideration for the transfer of a capital asset
Taxable under Profits and Gains of Business or Profession as a statutory business receipt
Taxable under Income from Other Sources as casual income
questions.explanation: Non-compete fees and any sum received under an agreement for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business or profession, or for not sharing any know-how, patent, copyright, trademark, or commercial right, are specifically taxable under PGBP.

questions.question: A trade association provides specialized technical product testing services exclusively to its member units for a specific testing fee. What is the taxability of this fee in the hands of the association?
options: Exempt from tax under the general principle of mutuality
Taxable under Income from House Property
Exempt provided the association is registered as a non-profit company
Taxable under Profits and Gains of Business or Profession as income from specific services performed for members
questions.explanation: Income derived by a trade, professional, or similar association from specific services performed for its members is specifically enumerated as income chargeable under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession'.

questions.question: A land dealer converts a commercial plot held as stock-in-trade (cost: ₹30,00,000) into a permanent capital asset when its Fair Market Value is ₹55,00,000. What is the tax consequence in the year of conversion?
options: The Fair Market Value of ₹55,00,000 is recognized, resulting in business profit of ₹25,00,000 taxable under PGBP in the year of conversion
No income arises until the converted capital asset is subsequently sold to a third party
₹25,00,000 is taxable as Long Term Capital Gain in the year of conversion
The entire ₹55,00,000 is taxable as casual income under Income from Other Sources
questions.explanation: Under the deeming provisions of PGBP, the Fair Market Value of inventory on the date on which it is converted into a capital asset is chargeable as business income under PGBP. The business profit is FMV minus cost (₹55,00,000 - ₹30,00,000 = ₹25,00,000).

questions.question: A sole distributor receives ₹20,00,000 as compensation for the premature cancellation of its nationwide distribution agency. The distributor claims the compensation is a capital receipt for loss of business apparatus. Is this claim valid?
options: Valid, because compensation for total sterilisation of a profit-making apparatus is a non-taxable capital receipt
Invalid, because compensation in connection with the termination or modification of terms of any business contract is statutory PGBP income, whether revenue or capital in nature
Valid, provided the distributor closes its business within 30 days of receiving compensation
Invalid, because such compensation is mandatorily taxable under Capital Gains
questions.explanation: Any compensation or other payment received in connection with the termination or modification of the terms and conditions of any contract relating to business is statutorily chargeable to tax under PGBP, irrespective of whether the receipt is of a revenue or capital nature.

questions.question: A corporate entity owns 20 residential apartments and lets them out on lease, maintaining dedicated property managers. Following the statutory amendment by Finance Act 2024, under which head should this residential rental income be assessed?
options: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession, because leasing is conducted as a structured commercial business activity
Income from Other Sources, as residential rental receipts cannot fall under any specific head
Income from House Property, because letting out of a residential house or part thereof by the owner is excluded from PGBP and taxable under IFHP
Exempt income, provided the company creates a dedicated housing infrastructure reserve
questions.explanation: As per the statutory Explanation added to Section 28 by Finance Act 2024, any income from letting out of a residential house or a part of the house by the owner shall not be taxable under 'PGBP' and shall be taxable under 'Income from house property', irrespective of corporate objects or business scale.

questions.question: Under what statutory condition is a commercial transaction in commodities or shares classified as a speculative transaction for tax purposes?
options: When the transaction is executed on an unrecognised regional commodity exchange
When the transaction results in an overall trading loss exceeding standard commercial gross margin
When the transaction involves dematerialized securities held for less than 30 days
When the transaction is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by actual physical delivery or transfer of the commodity or scrips
questions.explanation: A speculative transaction is defined as a transaction in which a contract for the purchase or sale of any commodity, including stocks and shares, is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by actual delivery or transfer. Speculative business is treated as a separate and distinct business.

questions.question: A textile manufacturer enters into forward contracts to purchase raw cotton bales to protect its spinning mills against anticipated future price rises. How is this transaction treated for income-tax purposes?
options: It is deemed a non-speculative hedging transaction entered into to guard against price fluctuations in raw materials used in the manufacturing business
It is deemed a speculative transaction because physical settlement occurs at a future date
It is an inadmissible contingent expenditure disallowed under business deductions
It is chargeable under Capital Gains rather than PGBP
questions.explanation: A hedging contract entered into in respect of raw materials or merchandise by a person in the course of manufacturing or merchanting business to guard against loss through future price fluctuations is statutorily deemed NOT to be a speculative transaction.

questions.question: A share dealer enters into forward contracts in equity shares to guard against loss through price fluctuations in stock-in-trade holdings. What is the tax classification of this forward contract?
options: Speculative transaction, because share price movements cannot be physically insured
Deemed non-speculative transaction entered into by an investor/dealer to protect stock-in-trade holdings against price volatility
Void transaction under security contract regulations and disallowed
Short Term Capital Gain transaction outside business income
questions.explanation: A contract entered into by a dealer or investor in stocks and shares to guard against loss in their holding of stocks and shares through price fluctuations is expressly deemed not to be a speculative transaction.

questions.question: An investor trades in Nifty and Bank Nifty derivative futures on the National Stock Exchange through a registered broker with digital contract notes. What is the tax classification of this trading activity?
options: Speculative business, because derivative contracts are settled on cash differences without physical equity delivery
Gambling and wagering transaction chargeable at a flat 30% rate without loss set-off
Non-speculative business transaction, because eligible derivative trading on a recognised stock exchange is statutory excluded from speculative transactions
Exclusively assessable under Capital Gains
questions.explanation: Trading in derivatives carried out in a recognized stock exchange is statutorily deemed NOT to be a speculative transaction.

questions.question: A trader carries out derivative transactions in agricultural commodities on a recognized commodity stock exchange where Commodity Transaction Tax (CTT) was not charged. Is this transaction treated as speculative?
options: Speculative, because payment of CTT is a mandatory condition for all commodity derivative exceptions
Illegal commodity wagering transaction with 100% penalty
Speculative only if the contract results in a net gain
Non-speculative, because the statutory requirement of CTT chargeability does not apply to trading in agricultural commodity derivatives
questions.explanation: Trading in commodity derivatives through a recognized stock exchange on which CTT is paid is deemed non-speculative. However, the requirement of CTT chargeability is explicitly NOT applicable in respect of trading in agricultural commodity derivatives.

questions.question: In K & Co., what principle was laid down by the Delhi High Court regarding interest earned on fixed deposits pledged as margin money for business bank guarantees?
options: Interest earned on bank deposits inextricably linked to the business operations of the assessee is taxable under PGBP and not under Income from Other Sources
Interest on bank fixed deposits is always assessable under Income from Other Sources regardless of business necessity
Interest on bank guarantee margin money is totally exempt from income-tax as a statutory cost reimbursement
Interest must be reduced from the contract execution cost without income recognition
questions.explanation: In K & Co., the Delhi High Court held that where the assessee was required to deposit margin money with a bank for obtaining a bank guarantee essential for the assessee's business, the interest earned on such deposits is inextricably linked to the business and must be taxed under PGBP, not IFOS.

questions.question: A construction company has surplus idle cash of ₹50,00,000 and places it in 1-year bank fixed deposits. Simultaneously, it places ₹10,00,000 in fixed deposits as compulsory margin money for obtaining a performance bank guarantee for a highway contract. How should the interest from these two deposits be classified?
options: Entire interest from both deposits is taxable under PGBP
Interest on the ₹10,00,000 mandatory margin deposit is taxable under PGBP (inextricably linked), while interest on the ₹50,00,000 surplus deposit is taxable under IFOS
Entire interest from both deposits is taxable under Income from Other Sources
Both interest amounts are exempt from income-tax
questions.explanation: Applying the ratio of K & Co. (Delhi HC), interest on margin money compulsorily deposited for essential business bank guarantees is inextricably linked to business and taxable under PGBP. Conversely, interest earned on surplus/idle funds placed in deposits is assessable under Income from Other Sources.

questions.question: In Chennai Properties & Investment Ltd, what critical test was established by the Supreme Court to hold that rental income was assessable under PGBP rather than Income from House Property?
options: Whether the company employed full-time property maintenance staff
Whether the leases were registered under municipal commercial establishment acts
Whether acquiring, holding, and letting properties constituted the main objective of the company as per its Memorandum of Association and represented its primary business activity
Whether rent was received through electronic banking channels
questions.explanation: In Chennai Properties & Investment Ltd, the Supreme Court held that where holding and letting properties is the main corporate objective in the Memorandum of Association and the company's entire activity consists of letting such properties, the letting activity is a business activity taxable under PGBP.

questions.question: Commercial Malls Ltd is formed with the primary objective in its MOA to hold and lease commercial office complexes and derives rental income from leasing shop lots. How does Chennai Properties apply post Finance Act 2024?
options: The ruling is entirely overridden, making all rental income taxable under IFHP
Commercial rental income must be apportioned 50:50 between PGBP and IFOS
Commercial letting is assessable under Capital Gains
The ruling continues to govern commercial properties where letting is the core MOA objective (PGBP), while residential property letting by owners is statutorily excluded and taxed under IFHP
questions.explanation: Following the Finance Act 2024 amendment (which specifically mandates that letting out of residential houses by the owner is taxable under IFHP), the Chennai Properties ratio applies to commercial properties where letting is the primary MOA objective, taxing commercial rents under PGBP.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the deductibility of rent, rates, and taxes of a building between an owner and a tenant under Section 30?
options: Rent is deductible for a tenant but not for an owner; Rates & Taxes and Insurance are deductible for both owner and tenant
Rent and Rates & Taxes are deductible for both owner and tenant without restriction
Owner can claim rent paid to himself as a notional business deduction
Tenant can claim rent and rates but cannot claim building insurance
questions.explanation: Under Section 30, a tenant can claim deduction for rent, rates & taxes, insurance, and revenue repairs. An owner occupying the building for business cannot claim rent (no notional rent to self), but can claim rates & taxes, insurance, and revenue repairs.

questions.question: A tenant incurs ₹20,00,000 on structural capital renovations and civil additions to a leased factory building. How is this capital expenditure treated under PGBP?
options: Allowed as an immediate 100% revenue deduction under rent, rates, and repairs
Disallowed as a revenue deduction, but treated as a 'Deemed Building' on which the tenant is entitled to claim depreciation under Section 32
Added to the landlord's block of assets with zero tax benefit to the tenant
Treated as an inadmissible personal loss of capital
questions.explanation: Under Section 30 and Explanation 1 to Section 32(1), capital expenditure incurred on renovation or improvement of a leased building by a tenant is disallowed as a revenue deduction, but is treated as a Deemed Building owned by the tenant, eligible for depreciation under Section 32.

questions.question: A manufacturing company incurs ₹5,00,000 on current revenue overhaul of its machines and ₹12,00,000 on capital replacement of key engine blocks that substantially increase production capacity. What is the tax treatment?
options: Both ₹5,00,000 and ₹12,00,000 are deductible as current revenue repairs under Section 31
Both expenditures are 100% disallowed because machinery repairs must be amortized over 5 years
₹5,00,000 is allowed as a revenue deduction u/s 31; ₹12,00,000 is disallowed as a revenue deduction and must be capitalized to the Block of Assets for claiming depreciation
₹12,00,000 is allowed as revenue deduction while ₹5,00,000 is capitalized
questions.explanation: Under Section 31, only current revenue repairs and insurance for plant and machinery are allowable deductions. Capital repairs are disallowed as revenue deductions and must be capitalized to the Block of Assets for depreciation.

questions.question: A partnership firm operates its administrative office in a commercial building owned personally by one of its partners and pays monthly rent to the partner. Is this rent deductible for the firm?
options: Completely disallowed because transactions between partners and firms are internal transfers
Allowed only if the partner pays tax at the maximum marginal rate of 30%
Deductible only up to a fixed statutory limit of ₹10,000 per month
Allowed as a deduction to the firm to the extent it is reasonable and not excessive having regard to market rates
questions.explanation: Rent paid by a partnership firm to a partner for using premises owned by the partner is an admissible business deduction under Section 30, subject to Section 40A(2) reasonableness limits (i.e. allowed to the extent not excessive).

questions.question: Under which provision of the Income-tax Act is rent paid for hiring plant and machinery deductible as a business expense?
options: Under Section 37 as a general business expenditure, because Section 31 covers only repairs and insurance of plant and machinery
Specifically under Section 31
Under Section 30 along with building rent
Under Section 32 as an element of notional depreciation
questions.explanation: Section 31 covers only insurance and current repairs of plant, machinery, and furniture. Rent for hiring plant and machinery is deductible as a general business expenditure under Section 37(1).

questions.question: Which of the following conditions must be satisfied for an assessee to claim depreciation under Section 32?
options: The assessee must possess registered legal title AND the asset must be actively operated for at least 300 days
The assessee must be the legal or beneficial owner (wholly or partly) AND the asset must be used for the purpose of business or profession (active or passive)
The asset must be completely paid for in cash without any outstanding bank loans
The asset must be manufactured in India and installed in an approved industrial zone
questions.explanation: Under Section 32, depreciation is allowable if: (1) The assessee is the owner (wholly or partly, legal or beneficial); and (2) The asset is used for the purposes of the assessee's business or profession (which includes active or passive use).

questions.question: A buyer purchases an industrial building, takes full possession, pays the entire purchase price, and operates its factory in the building, but the formal registration deed is pending. Can the buyer claim depreciation?
options: No, because legal registration of the conveyance deed is an absolute pre-condition for tax depreciation
Depreciation is available only to the seller until registration is completed
Yes, because beneficial ownership with possession and operational control is sufficient to claim depreciation under Section 32
Depreciation is restricted to 50% until legal title is formally registered
questions.explanation: For Section 32, beneficial ownership suffices. An assessee who has acquired possession and paid consideration in part performance of a contract is the beneficial owner entitled to claim depreciation, even without a registered title deed.

questions.question: An assessee acquires machinery on hire purchase. The agreement specifies that legal ownership will pass only upon payment of the 48th and final monthly instalment. From which year can the assessee claim depreciation?
options: Only after paying the 48th instalment and obtaining legal ownership
Depreciation cannot be claimed by either party throughout the hire term
Depreciation must be split 50:50 with the hire vendor
From the first previous year in which the asset is put to use, treating the hire purchaser as beneficial owner from inception
questions.explanation: In hire purchase transactions, the buyer is treated as the beneficial owner from inception and can claim depreciation from the first year the asset is put to use, even though legal ownership passes only upon payment of the last instalment.

questions.question: A power plant keeps standby turbines and emergency spares in complete operational readiness. During the previous year, the standby turbines were not actively run because the main turbines functioned without interruption. Is depreciation allowable?
options: Allowed, because passive use and operational readiness of standby machinery and emergency spares satisfy the 'used for business' condition
Disallowed, because Section 32 requires active operational wear and tear
Restricted to 10% of the prescribed depreciation rate
Allowed only if the main turbines suffer an operational breakdown
questions.explanation: For Section 32 depreciation, 'use' includes passive use. In the case of standby machinery and emergency spares kept ready for use, depreciation is allowable even if they are not actively operated during the year.

questions.question: In the landmark ruling of ICDS Ltd, what ratio did the Supreme Court lay down regarding depreciation on leased vehicles registered in the name of the lessee?
options: Depreciation is available only to the person holding vehicular registration under the Motor Vehicles Act
Depreciation is allowable to the lessor who holds exclusive ownership rights and repossession powers under the lease agreement, even if the vehicle is registered in the name of the lessee
Depreciation must be split equally between lessor and lessee
Leased vehicles are non-depreciable inventory
questions.explanation: In ICDS Ltd, the Supreme Court held that depreciation is allowable to the lessor where the lease agreement establishes that the lessor is the exclusive owner with inspection and repossession rights, notwithstanding that the vehicle is registered in the lessee's name.

questions.question: A commercial fleet leasing company leases trucks under finance lease contracts. The trucks are registered with the RTO in the lessees' names to comply with transport permits. The Assessing Officer denies depreciation to the lessor citing lessee registration. Is the AO's action justified?
options: Justified, because vehicular registration under the Motor Vehicles Act is conclusive proof of ownership for Section 32
Justified, unless the lessor operates the transport routes directly
Unjustified, because under ICDS Ltd, substantive ownership lies in the terms of the lease agreement, entitling the lessor to depreciation regardless of administrative RTO registration
Unjustified only if the vehicles are used within special economic zones
questions.explanation: Applying ICDS Ltd (SC), the lessor who retains exclusive contractual ownership, inspection rights, and repossession rights upon default is entitled to claim depreciation under Section 32, notwithstanding that the vehicle is registered in the lessee's name for regulatory convenience.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches the prescribed rates of depreciation for assets under the Income-tax Rules?
options: Residential Building: 10%; Commercial Building: 15%; Computers: 60%
Plant & Machinery General: 20%; Motor cars in hiring business: 15%
Intangible assets: 40%; Computer accessories: 15%
Residential Building: 5%; Commercial Building: 10%; Temporary Wooden Structures: 40%; Furniture: 10%
questions.explanation: Under the depreciation rate schedule: Buildings — Residential (5%), Commercial/Other (10%), Temporary wooden structures (40%); Furniture & fittings (10%); General P&M (15%); Computers & computer software (40%); Intangibles (25%).

questions.question: An IT company acquires mobile smartphones and an EPABX telephone exchange for its call center operations. At what rate is depreciation allowable on these devices?
options: 15%, because EPABX systems and mobile phones are communication apparatus and not computers
40%, because smartphones and digital exchanges are computing devices
25%, as intangible communication assets
10%, as office furniture and fittings
questions.explanation: EPABX systems and mobile phones are communication devices, NOT computers; hence they are eligible for the general Plant & Machinery depreciation rate of 15%, not the 40% computer rate.

questions.question: As per the statutory definition under Section 43(3), which of the following items is EXCLUDED from the scope of 'Plant'?
options: Ships and technical books used in professional libraries
Tea bushes, livestock, buildings, and furniture
Scientific apparatus and surgical equipment
Pollution control equipment and renewable energy devices
questions.explanation: Section 43(3) defines 'plant' to include ships, vehicles, books, scientific apparatus, and surgical equipment used for business or profession, but specifically EXCLUDES tea bushes, livestock, buildings, and furniture.

questions.question: Which of the following intangible assets is specifically EXCLUDED from claiming 25% depreciation under Section 32?
options: Know-how and patents
Copyrights and trademarks
Goodwill of a business or profession
Commercial licences and business franchises
questions.explanation: Intangible assets eligible for 25% depreciation include know-how, patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, franchises, or other commercial rights of similar nature, but explicitly EXCLUDE goodwill of a business or profession.

questions.question: An assessee deliberately omits claiming depreciation in its Return of Income to report higher business profits and avoid book profit minimum taxes. What is the statutory consequence?
options: The Assessing Officer is bound to accept the return without any depreciation allowance
The assessee is penalized with a 200% penalty for under-reporting income
The entire Block of Assets is deemed dissolved
Depreciation is mandatory; the AO shall compute and allow depreciation, and the Closing WDV of the Block is reduced by notional depreciation actually allowable
questions.explanation: Claiming depreciation is mandatory for all assessees. Explanation 5 to Section 32(1) provides that the provisions of Section 32 apply whether or not the assessee has claimed the deduction in computing total income.

questions.question: Which category of assessees has the statutory option to calculate depreciation under the Straight Line Method (SLM) on individual assets instead of the WDV Block of Assets method?
options: Assessees engaged in the business of generation or generation and distribution of power
All micro, small, and medium manufacturing enterprises
Companies listed on recognized stock exchanges
Export oriented units located in Special Economic Zones
questions.explanation: Only undertakings engaged in the generation or generation and distribution of power have the statutory option to follow the Straight Line Method (SLM) on individual assets. All other assessees must follow the WDV method on Block of Assets.

questions.question: What is the statutory definition of a 'Block of Assets' under Section 2(11)?
options: A group of assets acquired in the same financial year from a single vendor
A group of assets falling within a class of assets in respect of which the same rate of depreciation is prescribed
All tangible assets located within a single manufacturing factory compound
Assets whose individual historical cost exceeds ₹1,00,000
questions.explanation: A Block of Assets means a group of assets falling within a class of assets (e.g. buildings, machinery, furniture, or intangibles) in respect of which the same percentage rate of depreciation is prescribed.

questions.question: An assessee acquires a new machine for ₹5,00,000 during the previous year on 10th August but does not put it to use during that previous year. How is this machine treated in computing WDV and depreciation for that year?
options: It is excluded from the Block of Assets entirely until the year it is put to use
Full 15% depreciation is allowable because it was acquired before 3rd October
It is added to the Block of Assets for computing WDV, but no depreciation is allowed on that machine for the current previous year
50% depreciation is allowed as an idle asset
questions.explanation: An asset acquired during the previous year is added to the Block of Assets, but if it is not put to use during that previous year, no depreciation is allowable on that specific asset for the current previous year.

questions.question: A company sells an office building forming part of its 10% building block for an actual sale price of ₹60,00,000, while the Stamp Duty Value (SDV) adopted by state authorities is ₹80,00,000. What amount is deducted from the Block of Assets?
options: ₹80,00,000, because Stamp Duty Value is mandatory for all real estate adjustments
₹70,00,000, being the average of actual price and SDV
Nil, because buildings cannot be removed from a Block until all units are sold
₹60,00,000, because only the actual sale price (money payable) is reduced from the Block of Assets
questions.explanation: For adjusting the Block of Assets under Section 32, only the actual sale price (money payable) is reduced from the Block. Stamp Duty Value is considered only when computing capital gains under Section 50 / Section 50C.

questions.question: A manufacturer acquires a machine on 1st November of Year 1 and puts it to use for 151 days in Year 1. In Year 2, the machine is operated for only 90 days due to maintenance. What rate of depreciation applies in Year 1 and Year 2?
options: Year 1: 50% of normal rate; Year 2: 100% full normal rate, because the 50% restriction applies only in the year of acquisition
Year 1: 50% of normal rate; Year 2: 50% of normal rate (used <180 days in both years)
Year 1: Nil depreciation; Year 2: Full depreciation
Year 1: Full depreciation; Year 2: Pro-rata 90/365 depreciation
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Section 32(1), depreciation is restricted to 50% of the prescribed rate only in the previous year in which the asset is acquired and put to use for less than 180 days. In subsequent years, full depreciation is allowable even if used for less than 180 days.

questions.question: A firm acquires an asset in Year 1 (not put to use in Year 1). The asset is first put to use on 1st December of Year 2 (used for 121 days in Year 2). What depreciation is allowable in Year 1 and Year 2?
options: Year 1: Nil; Year 2: Restricted to 50% of normal rate
Year 1: Nil (not put to use); Year 2: Full 100% depreciation rate, because Year 2 is not the year of acquisition
Year 1: 50% rate; Year 2: 50% rate
Year 1: Full rate; Year 2: Full rate
questions.explanation: In Year 1, no depreciation is allowable as the asset was not put to use. In Year 2, since the year of acquisition was Year 1, the 50% restriction under the proviso to Section 32(1) does not apply because the restriction applies strictly when the asset is acquired and put to use for <180 days in the same year. Hence, full depreciation is allowed in Year 2.

questions.question: Company A amalgamates with Company B on 1st October during the previous year. How is normal depreciation computed and distributed between the two companies for that year?
options: Both Company A and Company B claim 100% full depreciation independently
Company A claims 50% and Company B claims 50% regardless of actual operational days
Total normal depreciation is computed as if no amalgamation took place, and then apportioned between Company A and Company B in the ratio of the number of days the assets were used by each
Depreciation is allowable exclusively to the amalgamated company (Company B)
questions.explanation: Under the fifth proviso to Section 32(1), in cases of amalgamation, demerger, or succession, total depreciation is calculated as if no restructuring occurred, and is then apportioned between predecessor and successor in the ratio of the number of days assets were used by them.

questions.question: An assessee has an opening WDV of ₹8,00,000 (3 machines). During the year, it sells all 3 machines for ₹5,00,000 and acquires no new machines. What is the tax result?
options: ₹3,00,000 Long Term Capital Loss, provided the machines were held for over 36 months
₹3,00,000 is carried forward as closing WDV on which 15% depreciation continues
No tax consequence until the assessee purchases a replacement machine
₹3,00,000 Short Term Capital Loss, because the Block ceases to exist and has a positive balance
questions.explanation: Under Section 50, where all assets in a Block are transferred (Block ceases to exist) and the Money Payable (₹5,00,000) is less than (Opening WDV + Additions = ₹8,00,000), the resulting shortfall of ₹3,00,000 is assessed as Short Term Capital Loss (STCL). No depreciation is allowed.

questions.question: An assessee has an opening WDV of ₹6,00,000 (5 machines). During the year, it sells 2 machines for ₹9,00,000, leaving 3 machines in the factory. What is the tax result?
options: ₹3,00,000 Short Term Capital Gain, and the closing WDV of the Block becomes Nil
₹3,00,000 Long Term Capital Gain, and depreciation continues on the remaining 3 machines
Closing WDV becomes negative ₹3,00,000 on which negative depreciation is charged
No capital gain arises because assets are still physically present in the Block
questions.explanation: Under Section 50, where Money Payable (₹9,00,000) exceeds (Opening WDV + Additions = ₹6,00,000), the excess of ₹3,00,000 is assessed as Short Term Capital Gain (STCG). The closing WDV becomes Nil and no depreciation is allowable, even though 3 machines remain physically present.

questions.question: Which of the following business entities is eligible to claim additional depreciation under Section 32(1)(ia)?
options: A trading partnership firm engaged in wholesale distribution of consumer goods
An assessee engaged in the business of manufacture or production of any article or thing, or generation/transmission/distribution of power
A telecommunication service provider operating cellular towers
A commercial bank providing leasing and credit facilities
questions.explanation: Additional depreciation @20% on new Plant & Machinery is available to assessees engaged in the manufacture or production of any article or thing, or in the generation, transmission, or distribution of power.

questions.question: On which of the following categories of plant and machinery is additional depreciation under Section 32(1)(ia) PROHIBITED?
options: New manufacturing machinery installed inside a factory shed
Pollution control equipment installed in manufacturing units
Second-hand machinery, office appliances, ships, aircraft, road transport vehicles, and P&M with 100% PGBP deduction
Material handling conveyor belts used on the assembly line
questions.explanation: Additional depreciation is not allowable on: (1) Second-hand P&M; (2) P&M installed in office premises or guest houses; (3) Office appliances and computers in office; (4) Ships, aircraft, and road transport vehicles; and (5) P&M on which 100% deduction is allowed under PGBP.

questions.question: A manufacturing company acquires and puts to use new factory machinery on 15th November (used for 137 days in Year 1). How is the 20% additional depreciation claimed?
options: 10% in Year 1, and the remaining 10% lapses permanently
Zero additional depreciation in Year 1, and full 20% in Year 2
Full 20% additional depreciation in Year 1 itself
10% in Year 1, and the remaining 10% is allowed in the immediately succeeding previous year (Year 2)
questions.explanation: Under the third proviso to Section 32(1)(ia), if new P&M is put to use for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition, 50% of the additional depreciation (10%) is allowed in that year, and the remaining 50% (10%) is allowed in the immediately succeeding previous year.

questions.question: A publishing house is engaged in printing newspapers and textbooks. Is it eligible for additional depreciation under Section 32(1)(ia)?
options: Eligible, because printing or printing and publishing is treated as a manufacturing business eligible for additional depreciation (CBDT)
Ineligible, because printing is a service activity rather than manufacturing
Eligible only if it exports 100% of its publications overseas
Ineligible unless it manufactures its own newsprint paper from pulp
questions.explanation: As per CBDT clarification, the business of printing or printing and publishing is treated as the manufacture or production of an article or thing, making new P&M eligible for additional depreciation under Section 32(1)(ia).

questions.question: A factory acquires new motorized forklift trucks to transport heavy raw material pallets between manufacturing bays within the factory compound. The AO disallows additional depreciation citing the transport vehicle exclusion. Is the AO correct?
options: Correct, because all motorized wheeled vehicles are excluded transport vehicles
Incorrect, because forklift trucks used inside factory premises for internal handling are plant and machinery and not road transport vehicles, making them eligible for additional depreciation
Correct, unless the forklift trucks are driven by solar energy
Incorrect only if the forklifts are operated by female technicians
questions.explanation: Forklift trucks used inside factory premises for internal material handling are plant & machinery integral to manufacturing, and are NOT road transport vehicles. Hence, they are eligible for additional depreciation @20%.

questions.question: A power generation undertaking opts for the Straight Line Method (SLM) on individual assets under Section 32(1)(i). Can it claim additional depreciation under Section 32(1)(ia)?
options: Yes, all power generating units are entitled to additional depreciation @20%
Yes, but the rate of additional depreciation under SLM is restricted to 10%
No, additional depreciation is available only to assessees opting for the WDV method; power units opting for SLM are not eligible
Yes, provided the power plant utilizes renewable wind energy
questions.explanation: Additional depreciation under Section 32(1)(ia) is allowable only if the assessee follows the WDV method. Power units opting for the Straight Line Method (SLM) under Section 32(1)(i) are not eligible for additional depreciation.

questions.question: Which of the following items forms part of the 'Actual Cost' of a newly acquired manufacturing machine under Section 43(1)?
options: Taxes and duties in respect of which Input Tax Credit (ITC) is admissible
Interest on loan incurred after the date the machine was put to commercial use
Government grants received specifically for purchasing the machine
Purchase price, transportation charges, installation expenses, and interest on capital borrowed up to the date the machine is first put to use
questions.explanation: Under Section 43(1), actual cost includes purchase cost, freight, installation charges, net trial run costs, and loan interest up to the date of first put to use. Duties where ITC is claimed and government grants are excluded/deducted.

questions.question: An assessee acquires a commercial generator for ₹3,50,000. It pays ₹3,35,000 by RTGS and pays ₹15,000 in cash on the same day to the vendor. What is the Actual Cost of the generator for depreciation u/s 43(1)?
options: ₹3,35,000, because payments made to a person in a day exceeding ₹10,000 otherwise than by specified banking channels are excluded from actual cost
₹3,50,000, because incidental cash payments under ₹20,000 are admissible
Nil, because any cash payment invalidates the entire capital asset cost
₹3,40,000, allowing a standard statutory cash deduction of ₹5,000
questions.explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 43(1), any expenditure for acquisition of an asset paid to a person in a day exceeding ₹10,000 otherwise than by account payee cheque, DD, or ECS is excluded from actual cost. Hence, Actual Cost = ₹3,50,000 - ₹15,000 = ₹3,35,000.

questions.question: A scientific research asset (cost: ₹10,00,000) on which 100% deduction was claimed u/s 35 is subsequently brought into regular manufacturing business. What is its Actual Cost for regular depreciation?
options: ₹10,00,000, being the historical acquisition cost
NIL, because 100% deduction was already allowed in full under Section 35
Fair Market Value on the date it is brought into regular business
₹10,00,000 minus notional depreciation for intermediate years
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 1 to Section 43(1), where an asset previously used for scientific research is brought into regular business, its Actual Cost to the assessee is NIL, because the entire capital expenditure was already deducted u/s 35.

questions.question: Where trading stock is converted into a capital asset and introduced into business operations, what is its Actual Cost under Explanation 1A to Section 43(1)?
options: Historical purchase cost of the inventory
Zero, until the asset is put to active use for 180 days
Fair Market Value of the inventory on the date of conversion (which was charged to tax under Section 28)
Lower of cost or net realizable value
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 1A to Section 43(1), where inventory is converted into a capital asset and used for business, its Actual Cost is the Fair Market Value on the date of conversion which was recognized as income u/s 28.

questions.question: An assessee acquires an industrial machine by way of inheritance. The previous owner had purchased it for ₹8,00,000 and claimed ₹3,00,000 depreciation before death. What is the Actual Cost to the heir?
options: ₹8,00,000, being original purchase cost
NIL, because inherited assets have zero monetary cost to the recipient
Fair Market Value on the date of inheritance
₹5,00,000, being actual cost to the previous owner minus depreciation actually allowed to the previous owner
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 2 to Section 43(1), where an asset is acquired by gift or inheritance, the Actual Cost to the assessee is the actual cost to the previous owner less depreciation actually allowed to the previous owner (i.e. ₹8,00,000 - ₹3,00,000 = ₹5,00,000).

questions.question: Under Explanation 3 to Section 43(1), what power does the Assessing Officer possess if an asset is acquired with the main purpose of claiming higher depreciation?
options: The AO can determine the Actual Cost of the asset (normally FMV), with the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner
The AO can seize the asset without notice
The AO can disallow 100% of the depreciation permanently
The AO can reclassify the asset as personal property
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 3 to Section 43(1), where an asset is acquired with the intention of claiming higher depreciation by inflating cost, the AO may, with the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner, determine the actual cost having regard to all circumstances (normally FMV).

questions.question: An assessee sells a machine (WDV at sale: ₹4,00,000) for ₹6,00,000 and re-acquires the same machine after 6 months for ₹7,50,000. What is the Actual Cost on re-acquisition?
options: ₹7,50,000, being the re-acquisition purchase price
₹4,00,000, being the lower of WDV at the time of sale (₹4,00,000) or re-acquisition price (₹7,50,000)
₹6,00,000, being the intermediate sale consideration
NIL
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 4 to Section 43(1), upon re-acquisition of an asset previously sold, Actual Cost is the lower of (1) WDV at the time of original sale, or (2) Re-acquisition cost. Hence, Actual Cost = ₹4,00,000.

questions.question: An individual purchases a residential house for ₹20,00,000 and uses it exclusively for personal residence for 3 years. Thereafter, the building is brought into business as an office. How is Actual Cost computed?
options: ₹20,00,000, without any deduction for past personal use
Fair Market Value of the building on the date of introduction into business
Original cost of ₹20,00,000 minus notional depreciation computed at current rates for the 3 intervening years
Zero, because personal assets brought into business cannot be depreciated
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 5 to Section 43(1), where a building previously used for personal/other purpose is brought into business, Actual Cost is original purchase cost minus notional depreciation computed at the rates in force for all intervening years.

questions.question: A holding company transfers a depreciable asset (WDV: ₹12,00,000) to its 100% Indian subsidiary company for ₹18,00,000. What is the Actual Cost to the subsidiary under Explanation 6 to Section 43(1)?
options: ₹18,00,000, being the consideration paid by the subsidiary
Fair Market Value on the date of transfer
Nil, as intra-group transfers are ignored
₹12,00,000, being the WDV to the transferor holding company
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 6 to Section 43(1), where a capital asset is transferred by a holding company to its 100% Indian subsidiary (or vice versa), the Actual Cost to the transferee is the WDV to the transferor company.

questions.question: A foreign non-resident brings an offshore drilling rig into India to execute a domestic contract. How is the Actual Cost of the rig determined under Explanation 11 to Section 43(1)?
options: Actual cost abroad minus depreciation calculated at Indian statutory rates as if the rig had been used in India since its acquisition
Original purchase cost of the rig abroad
Customs valuation adopted at the Indian seaport
NIL
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 11 to Section 43(1), where an asset acquired abroad by a non-resident is brought into India for business, Actual Cost is original cost minus depreciation calculated at the rates in force in India as if used in India since acquisition.

questions.question: An assessee uses a cold chain facility asset (cost: ₹50,00,000, 100% deduction claimed u/s 35AD) for 9 years in specified business and then transfers it to a non-specified business. What is the Actual Cost for the non-specified business?
options: NIL, because 100% deduction was allowed under Section 35AD and the transfer occurs after the mandatory 8-year period
Fair Market Value on the date of transfer
₹50,00,000 minus notional depreciation for 9 years
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 13 to Section 43(1), where an asset on which Section 35AD deduction was claimed is transferred to a non-specified business after the expiry of 8 years, the Actual Cost to the transferee/business is NIL.

questions.question: A tea manufacturing company derives composite income where only 40% is taxable under PGBP and 60% is exempt agricultural income. In computing WDV of its factory machinery under Explanation 7 to Section 43(6), what depreciation is deducted?
options: Only 40% of the total depreciation, representing the portion actually taxed
Zero depreciation is deducted to protect agricultural parity
100% of the computed depreciation, deemed as if the entire composite income was chargeable under PGBP
60% of the computed depreciation
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 7 to Section 43(6), in composite agricultural and business operations (Tea/Coffee/Rubber), for computing WDV, 100% of the depreciation is deducted as if the entire income were taxable under PGBP, deemed as actually allowed.

questions.question: A power generating company on SLM sells an individual generator (Cost: ₹100, WDV: ₹80) in year 3. What are the tax implications if it is sold for: (a) ₹72; (b) ₹89; (c) ₹117?
options: (a) ₹8 Capital Loss; (b) ₹9 STCG; (c) ₹37 STCG
(a) ₹8 Terminal Depreciation; (b) ₹9 Capital Gain; (c) ₹37 Balancing Charge
All sales under SLM are adjusted into Block WDV
(a) ₹8 Terminal Depreciation u/s 32(1)(iii); (b) ₹9 Balancing Charge u/s 41(2) (PGBP); (c) ₹20 Balancing Charge u/s 41(2) (PGBP) + ₹17 STCG u/s 50A
questions.explanation: Under SLM for power units: (a) Sale < WDV (₹72 < ₹80) -> ₹8 Terminal Depreciation allowed u/s 32(1)(iii); (b) WDV < Sale <= Cost (₹80 < ₹89 <= ₹100) -> ₹9 Balancing Charge taxable u/s 41(2); (c) Sale > Cost (₹117 > ₹100) -> ₹20 Balancing Charge up to cost taxable u/s 41(2) and excess ₹17 taxable as STCG u/s 50A.

questions.question: A business car (Opening WDV: ₹4,00,000, 15% rate) is used 60% for business and 40% for personal driving. How is depreciation and Closing WDV determined under Section 38(2)?
options: Depreciation allowed: ₹36,000 (60%); Disallowed: ₹24,000 (40%); Closing WDV reduced only by allowed depreciation of ₹36,000 to ₹3,64,000
Total depreciation ₹60,000 allowed in full; Closing WDV ₹3,40,000
Depreciation allowed: ₹36,000; Closing WDV reduced by full ₹60,000 to ₹3,40,000
Zero depreciation allowed on mixed-use vehicles
questions.explanation: Under Section 38(2), deductions for mixed-use assets are restricted proportionately (60% allowed = ₹36,000). While computing Closing WDV, only the depreciation actually allowed (₹36,000) is deducted from the Block, resulting in Closing WDV of ₹3,64,000.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly states the legal rules governing the carry-forward and set-off of unabsorbed depreciation under Section 32(2)?
options: Can be carried forward for a maximum of 8 assessment years and set off only against PGBP
Can be carried forward indefinitely, can be set off against any head of income except Salaries, and does not require the original business to be in existence
Can be set off only against Capital Gains of the same business
Lapses automatically if the business closes down
questions.explanation: Under Section 32(2), unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward indefinitely, can be set off against income under any head (except 'Salaries'), and can be set off even if the business to which it relates no longer exists.

questions.question: In what order of priority must an assessee adjust depreciation and business losses in any assessment year?
options: Brought forward business loss -> Current year depreciation -> Unabsorbed depreciation
Unabsorbed depreciation -> Current year depreciation -> Brought forward business loss
Current year depreciation -> Brought forward business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation
Current year depreciation -> Unabsorbed depreciation -> Brought forward business loss
questions.explanation: The mandatory statutory hierarchy of set-off in any assessment year is: (1) Current year depreciation; (2) Brought forward business loss; (3) Unabsorbed depreciation.

questions.question: How are government subsidies and grants treated under Section 2(24)(xviii) and Section 43(1)?
options: All subsidies are tax-free capital receipts
All subsidies must be credited to General Reserve without tax impact
Subsidies are taxable under Income from Other Sources only

General subsidies are taxable as PGBP income; subsidies specifically granted for acquiring a capital asset are reduced from the Actual Cost of that asset; trust corpus and individual welfare subsidies are exempt
questions.explanation: Under Section 2(24)(xviii), government grants, subsidies, and waivers are taxable as PGBP income. Under Explanation 10 to Section 43(1), if a subsidy is directly relatable to acquiring an asset, it is reduced from actual cost. Trust corpus and individual welfare subsidies are excluded.

questions.question: A company borrows capital to acquire new factory machinery. How is interest on this borrowed capital treated before and after the machine is put to use?
options: Interest up to the date of first put to use is added to Actual Cost; interest after first put to use is allowed as a deductible revenue expense u/s 36(1)(iii)
Entire interest across all years must be capitalized to Actual Cost
Entire interest is deductible as a revenue expense immediately upon payment
Interest is disallowed under Section 40(a)
questions.explanation: Interest on loan borrowed for acquiring a capital asset incurred up to the date the asset is first put to use must be capitalized to the Actual Cost of the asset. Interest incurred after the date of put to use is deductible as revenue expenditure u/s 36(1)(iii).

questions.question: What is the quantum of deduction available under Section 33AB for an assessee engaged in growing and manufacturing tea in India?
options: 100% of the amount deposited in any scheduled commercial bank
Actual amount deposited in NABARD account within 6 months of PY end or return filing due date, or 40% of PGBP (before this deduction), whichever is lower
20% of net agricultural turnover
Actual amount deposited in SBI Site Restoration account or 20% of PGBP, whichever is lower
questions.explanation: Under Section 33AB, the deduction is lower of: (1) Actual amount deposited in NABARD within 6 months from the end of the previous year or due date of filing return, whichever is earlier; or (2) 40% of PGBP profits (before this deduction). Form 3AC audit report is mandatory.

questions.question: An assessee in petroleum extraction deposits funds in the SBI Site Restoration Account. What is the maximum deduction allowed under Section 33ABA?
options: Lower of actual amount deposited or 40% of PGBP
100% of global oil turnover
Lower of actual amount deposited by the end of the previous year or 20% of PGBP before this deduction
₹10 Crore per oil field
questions.explanation: Under Section 33ABA, deduction is lower of: (1) Actual amount deposited in SBI Site Restoration Account up to the end of the previous year; or (2) 20% of PGBP profits (before this deduction). Form 3AD audit report is mandatory.

questions.question: What is the consequence if funds withdrawn from the NABARD account or Site Restoration Account are not utilized in the year of withdrawal or are utilized to buy office appliances?
options: Treated as an interest-free loan from the Board
Allowed as a deduction under Section 37
The entire business licence is canceled by the tax department
The unutilized/misutilized amount is deemed PGBP income and taxed in the year of withdrawal
questions.explanation: Any amount withdrawn from the special account must be utilized within the year of withdrawal for approved scheme purposes. If misutilized or utilized for office appliances/residential P&M, the deduction allowed earlier is withdrawn and deemed PGBP income.

questions.question: How does the tax treatment of outstanding deposit balances upon business closure or firm dissolution differ between Section 33AB and Section 33ABA?
options: Under Section 33AB, closure/dissolution is taxable (death/partition is not taxable); under Section 33ABA, all withdrawals net of government dues are fully taxable without exception
Both sections treat all closure withdrawals as completely tax-free
Section 33AB is exempt while Section 33ABA is taxable under Capital Gains
Both sections transfer deposits to the Central Government without income tax
questions.explanation: Under Section 33AB, withdrawals on business closure, dissolution of firm, or liquidation are taxable (withdrawals on death or HUF partition are not taxable). Under Section 33ABA, any amount withdrawn (minus amounts payable to Central Government) is fully taxable in the year of withdrawal without exception.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical manufacturing company incurs ₹25,00,000 on revenue scientific research and ₹60,00,000 on capital research (including ₹15,00,000 for purchasing land). What deduction is allowable under Section 35(1)(i) and Section 35(2)?
options: ₹85,00,000, covering all revenue and capital expenditures
₹70,00,000 (100% of revenue research ₹25L + 100% of capital research excluding land ₹45L)
₹45,00,000, as capital research is amortized over 5 years
Nil, unless the research produces a commercially patented drug
questions.explanation: Under Section 35, 100% deduction is allowed for revenue expenditure u/s 35(1)(i) and capital expenditure u/s 35(2) related to the assessee's business. However, cost of land is strictly EXCLUDED from Section 35 deduction. Thus, deduction = ₹25L + (₹60L - ₹15L) = ₹70,00,000.

questions.question: An assessee donates ₹5,00,000 to an approved national research laboratory. Subsequently, the Central Government withdraws approval from the laboratory. What happens to the donor's deduction under Section 35?
options: The deduction is withdrawn and reassessed with retrospective effect
The donor must claim deduction under Section 80G at 50%
The deduction shall not be denied to the donor if approval was withdrawn after payment of the sum
The donation is converted into a taxable capital asset
questions.explanation: Under Section 35 notes, deduction allowed for contributions to approved scientific research institutions/universities shall NOT be denied merely on the grounds that subsequent to the payment, the approval granted to such institution has been withdrawn.

questions.question: Under Section 35(1A), what statutory reporting requirement must be fulfilled for a donor to claim deduction for external scientific research contributions?
options: The donor must obtain physical signature from the jurisdictional Commissioner
The donation must be published in the Official Gazette
The donor must file a special research return in Form 3CD
The donee institution must prepare and submit Statement Form 10BD and furnish Certificate Form 10BE to the donor by 31st May of the succeeding FY
questions.explanation: Under Section 35(1A), the donor is entitled to deduction for research contributions only if the donee institution submits statement Form 10BD to tax authorities and furnishes certificate Form 10BE to the donor by 31st May of the next financial year.

questions.question: A scientific research machine (cost: ₹10,00,000, 100% deduction claimed u/s 35) is sold without being used for regular business for: (a) ₹8,00,000; (b) ₹14,00,000. What is the tax result?
options: (a) ₹2,00,000 Terminal Depreciation; (b) ₹4,00,000 Balancing Charge
Sale proceeds are completely exempt
questions.explanation: Under Section 41(3), when a scientific research asset is sold without regular business use: (a) Sale proceeds up to cost (₹8,00,000) are taxable as PGBP; (b) When sold for ₹14,00,000, amount up to cost (₹10,00,000) is taxable as PGBP u/s 41(3), and the excess over cost (₹4,00,000) is taxable under Capital Gains.

questions.question: A telecom company acquires a 10-year telecom licence/spectrum on 1st July of Year 1 for ₹1,10,00,000 (remaining licence life: 11 previous years including acquisition year). How is deduction claimed under Section 35ABB / 35ABA?
options: Depreciation @25% under Section 32 as an intangible asset
Amortized in equal annual instalments (₹10,00,000 per year) over the 11 previous years; no Section 32 depreciation allowed
100% upfront deduction in Year 1
Amortized over a mandatory 5-year block
questions.explanation: Under Section 35ABB (Licence) and Section 35ABA (Spectrum), fees paid are amortized in equal annual instalments over the remaining life of the licence/spectrum. Depreciation under Section 32 is strictly prohibited.

questions.question: Which assessee is eligible to claim 100% deduction for notified Skill Development Projects under Section 35CCD?
options: All resident individuals and HUFs
Partnership firms and LLPs
Only corporate assessees (Companies), excluding cost of Land & Building
All assessees including non-residents
questions.explanation: Deduction @100% under Section 35CCD for notified Skill Development Projects is available ONLY to Companies (excluding expenditure on Land & Building). Conversely, Section 35CCC for Agricultural Extension Projects is available to all assessees.

questions.question: In Ceebros Hotel Pvt. Ltd., what principle was established by the Madras High Court regarding Section 35AD deduction where star categorization approval was delayed by government authorities?
options: Deduction is permanently forfeited if the inspection certificate is dated in a subsequent year
Deduction is restricted to 50% for delayed approvals
The hotel must pay a compounding fine to regularize the deduction

Section 35AD is an incentive provision that must be interpreted liberally; an assessee cannot be penalized with denial of deduction in the commencement year merely due to departmental delay in issuing formal approval
questions.explanation: In Ceebros Hotel Pvt. Ltd., the Madras High Court held that Section 35AD is a beneficial infrastructure provision that must be liberally interpreted. Where the hotel was operational and applied for 3-star categorization in the PY, deduction cannot be denied merely because administrative approval was granted in the next year.

questions.question: Royal Resorts sets up a 3-star hotel and commences commercial operations in January. It applied for star categorization in February, but the tourism board conducted inspection and issued the star certificate in May of the next financial year. Can Royal Resorts claim Section 35AD deduction for the year of commencement?
options: Yes, applying Ceebros Hotel Pvt. Ltd., the approval relates back to the operational commencement year since the application was filed in time
No, deduction is available only starting from the year in which the certificate is physically dated
No, unless Royal Resorts obtains a special condonation order from the CBDT
Yes, but deduction is restricted to 20% of capital expenditure
questions.explanation: Applying Ceebros Hotel Pvt. Ltd. (Madras HC), since the hotel commenced operations and applied for 3-star approval within the relevant previous year, Section 35AD deduction cannot be denied in the year of commencement due to administrative delay by the granting authority.

questions.question: What is the maximum limit of preliminary expenses eligible for 5-year amortization under Section 35D for an Indian Company?
options: Lower of actual preliminary expenses or 5% of Cost of Project only
Lower of actual preliminary expenses or 5% of (Cost of Project or Capital Employed, whichever is higher)
100% of actual expenses without any monetary cap
10% of annual turnover
questions.explanation: Under Section 35D, for an Indian Company, eligible preliminary expenses are lower of actual expenses or 5% of Cost of Project (COP) or Capital Employed (CE), whichever is higher. For non-corporate residents, the limit is strictly 5% of Cost of Project.

questions.question: For computing the preliminary expense ceiling under Section 35D for an Indian company, what items are included in 'Capital Employed'?
options: Total assets minus current liabilities including revaluation reserves
Net worth plus short-term bank overdrafts
Issued share capital, debentures, and long-term borrowings as on the last day of the PY (excluding reserves, surplus, and securities premium)
Paid-up equity share capital only
questions.explanation: Capital Employed under Section 35D means the aggregate of issued share capital, debentures, and long-term borrowings as on the last day of the previous year. Reserves & Surplus (including securities premium) are explicitly EXCLUDED from Capital Employed.

questions.question: Under Section 35DD, how are expenses incurred by an Indian Company wholly and exclusively for amalgamation or demerger allowed as a deduction?
options: 100% upfront deduction in the year of restructuring
Disallowed as a capital restructuring loss
Amortized over 10 years
In 5 equal annual instalments beginning from the previous year in which amalgamation or demerger takes place
questions.explanation: Under Section 35DD, expenditure incurred by an Indian Company for amalgamation or demerger is allowed as a deduction in 5 equal annual instalments starting from the year in which the amalgamation/demerger takes place.

questions.question: An employer incurs ₹50,00,000 on voluntary retirement compensation paid to retiring employees. How is this expenditure deducted under Section 35DDA?
options: Deductible in 5 equal annual instalments of ₹10,00,000 each across all assessees
100% deductible in the year of payment under Section 37
Deductible in 10 equal instalments
Disallowed if the firm incurs a business loss
questions.explanation: Under Section 35DDA, any expenditure incurred by an assessee by way of payment of any sum to employees on voluntary retirement (VRS) is allowable as a deduction in 5 equal annual instalments.

questions.question: How is expenditure on prospecting and development of minerals deductible under Section 35E?
options: 100% upfront in the year prospecting begins
In 10 equal annual instalments starting from the year of commercial production, restricted to mining PGBP income
In 5 equal instalments without profit restrictions
Amortized over the physical life of the mine
questions.explanation: Under Section 35E, prospecting and mineral development expenses incurred in the commercial production year and 4 preceding years are deductible in 10 equal annual instalments, restricted to the PGBP income derived from the mining operations.

questions.question: Which of the following capital expenditures is EXCLUDED from claiming 100% deduction under Section 35AD?
options: Plant and machinery installed in an inland container depot
Civil construction of a cold storage warehouse
Cost of acquisition of Land, Goodwill, and Financial Instruments
Central air-conditioning systems for a 100-bed hospital
questions.explanation: Under Section 35AD, 100% deduction is allowed for all capital expenditures incurred for specified businesses, EXCEPT expenditure incurred on the acquisition of Land, Goodwill, and Financial Instruments.

questions.question: What are the statutory conditions regarding plant and machinery used in a Section 35AD specified business?
options: All machinery must be imported directly from OECD nations
100% of P&M must be brand new with zero second-hand components
Second-hand machinery can constitute up to 50% of total value
P&M must be new, with two exceptions: (1) Imported second-hand P&M not previously depreciated in India; and (2) Up to 20% of total P&M value can be domestic second-hand
questions.explanation: Under Section 35AD, the specified business must use new plant & machinery. Exceptions: (1) Previously imported second-hand P&M on which no depreciation was claimed in India; and (2) Up to 20% of the total value of plant & machinery can be second-hand.

questions.question: An assessee incurs a loss of ₹30,00,000 in a Section 35AD eligible 100-bed hospital business. Against what income can this loss be set off?
options: ONLY against profits of another specified business under Section 35AD (whether or not that other specified business is eligible for 35AD deduction)
Against profits of any business under PGBP or Long Term Capital Gains
Against income from house property and salaries
Cannot be set off in current year, but carried forward for maximum 8 years
questions.explanation: Under Section 73A, losses of a specified business u/s 35AD can be carried forward indefinitely and can ONLY be set off against profits of any other specified business (irrespective of whether the other specified business is eligible for 35AD deduction).

questions.question: A machine on which 100% deduction of ₹20,00,000 was claimed u/s 35AD is transferred to a regular non-specified business after 5 years. What is the tax consequence in the year of transfer?
options: The entire ₹20,00,000 is taxed as STCG

(Total 35AD deduction claimed minus Notional depreciation that would have been allowable for the 5 years) is taxable under PGBP; the resulting hypothetical WDV becomes the Actual Cost for the non-specified business
Zero tax impact because the asset was used for more than 3 years
The assessee must pay a 50% penalty on original cost
questions.explanation: Under Section 35AD(7B), if an asset is transferred to a non-specified business within 8 years, (35AD deduction claimed minus normal depreciation that would have been allowed) is taxable as PGBP income. Under Explanation 14 to Section 43(1), the resulting hypothetical WDV becomes its Actual Cost.

questions.question: A company issues Zero Coupon Bonds on 16th December redeemable after 10 months at a total discount of ₹22,00,000. How is the monthly discount amortized under Section 36(1)(iiia)?
options: Discount is deducted 100% in the year of redemption
Discount is divided by exactly 300 calendar days
Discount is amortized over 11 calendar months (period >=15 days in December rounded up to 1 full month), allowing 4 months' discount in that financial year
Discount is disallowed as a capital borrowing discount
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(iiia), discount on ZCBs is amortized pro-rata over the life of the bond in calendar months. If any calendar month fraction is 15 days or more, it is rounded up to 1 calendar month (<15 days ignored). Hence, 11 months life applies.

questions.question: An employer contributes ₹4,00,000 to a Recognized Provident Fund (RPF) and ₹2,00,000 to an Unrecognized Provident Fund (URPF). What is the deduction allowable under Section 36(1)(iv)?
options: ₹6,00,000, covering both funds
₹2,00,000 for URPF only
Nil, because employer contributions must be capitalized
₹4,00,000 for RPF (subject to Section 43B); the ₹2,00,000 contribution to URPF is strictly disallowed
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(iv)/(v), employer contributions to Statutory PF, Recognized PF, Approved Superannuation Fund, and Approved Gratuity Fund are deductible (subject to Section 43B). Contributions to Unrecognized/Unapproved funds are strictly disallowed.

questions.question: An employer contributes ₹3,00,000 to the NPS account of its employee u/s 80CCD. The employee's Basic Salary is ₹15,00,000 and DA (forming part of retirement benefits) is ₹5,00,000. What is the maximum deduction allowable to the employer under Section 36(1)(iva) following Finance Act 2024?
options: ₹3,00,000 (actual contribution in full)
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(iva) as amended by Finance Act 2024, employer contribution to NPS is deductible up to a maximum of 14% of Salary (Basic + DA retirement terms). 14% of ₹20,00,000 = ₹2,80,000 (lower of actual ₹3,00,000 or ₹2,80,000).

questions.question: What conditions must be satisfied to claim a deduction for Bad Debts under Section 36(1)(vii)?
options: The assessee must file a recovery suit in a civil court and obtain a court decree

The debt must be written off as irrecoverable in the accounts during the PY AND must have been taken into account in computing income of the current or earlier PY (no need to prove to AO that debt is irrecoverable)
The debtor must be declared officially insolvent by the NCLT
The debt must be older than 36 months
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(vii), bad debts are deductible if: (1) Written off as irrecoverable in the books of account of the assessee during the PY; and (2) The debt was included in computing total income of the current or earlier PY. The assessee is not required to establish that the debt has become irrecoverable.

questions.question: A commercial bank maintains a Provision for Bad & Doubtful Debts account with a credit balance of ₹15,00,000. During the year, it incurs actual bad debts of ₹22,00,000. What deduction is allowed under Section 36(1)(vii)?
options: ₹7,00,000, being the excess of actual bad debts (₹22L) over the provision account balance (₹15L)
Nil
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Section 36(1)(vii), for assessees maintaining a Provision for Bad & Doubtful Debts account u/s 36(1)(viia), actual bad debts must be debited to the provision account, and deduction u/s 36(1)(vii) is limited to the excess of actual bad debts over the provision balance.

questions.question: An assessee had claimed a bad debt deduction of ₹5,00,000 in Year 1. In Year 4, after closing down the business, the assessee unexpectedly recovers ₹3,50,000 from the debtor. What is the tax treatment under Section 41(4)?
options: Exempt from tax because the business was closed before recovery
Taxable under Capital Gains as recovery of a dead asset
Taxable under Income from Other Sources
₹3,50,000 is taxable as PGBP income in Year 4, even though the business is no longer in existence
questions.explanation: Under Section 41(4), where a deduction has been allowed in respect of a bad debt, any recovery made subsequently is deemed to be PGBP income in the year of recovery, even if the business or profession is no longer in existence in that year.

questions.question: A private limited company incurs ₹1,00,000 on medical camps (revenue) and ₹5,00,000 on constructing a staff healthcare clinic (capital) for promoting employee family planning. How is this deducted u/s 36(1)(ix)?
options: Revenue ₹1,00,000 is 100% deductible; Capital ₹5,00,000 is deductible in 5 equal annual instalments of ₹1,00,000 each (available only to Companies)
Entire ₹6,00,000 is 100% deductible upfront
Entire ₹6,00,000 is disallowed as personal staff expenditure
Deduction is available equally to partnership firms and individuals
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(ix), expenditure on promoting family planning amongst employees is allowable ONLY to corporate entities (Companies): Revenue expenditure is 100% deductible; Capital expenditure is deductible in 5 equal annual instalments. Non-corporates get nil deduction.

questions.question: Under what condition is Securities Transaction Tax (STT) or Commodities Transaction Tax (CTT) deductible under Section 36(1)(xv)/(xvi)?
options: Allowed for all capital asset investors holding shares for >12 months
Allowed only if the shares, units, or commodities are held as stock-in-trade
Allowed as a direct tax rebate against final tax payable
Disallowed under all circumstances
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(xv) and (xvi), STT and CTT paid in the course of business are deductible as business expenses ONLY if the underlying shares, units, or commodities are held as stock-in-trade (not as capital investments).

questions.question: How are Marked-to-Market (MTM) losses or expected future losses treated under Section 36(1)(xviii) and Section 40A(13)?
options: All expected and MTM losses are deductible based on accounting conservatism
MTM losses are deductible only by listed non-banking financial companies
MTM and expected losses are deductible ONLY if computed in accordance with notified ICDS; all other MTM/expected losses are expressly disallowed u/s 40A(13)
All MTM losses are taxable as deemed income
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(xviii) and Section 40A(13), any marked-to-market loss or other expected loss is allowable ONLY if computed in accordance with notified Income Computation and Disclosure Standards (ICDS). All other MTM losses are disallowed.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions must be concurrently satisfied for an expenditure to be deductible under Section 37(1)?
options: Expenditure authorized by a resolution passed at an Extraordinary General Meeting
Expenditure paid in foreign currency with RBI approval
Expenditure resulting in an enduring tangible physical asset
Expenditure not covered u/s 30 to 36, incurred wholly and exclusively for business/profession, revenue in nature, not personal, and incurred for a legal purpose
