questions.explanation: Under Section 37(1), any expenditure not covered under Sections 30 to 36 is deductible if: (1) Incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business or profession; (2) Revenue in nature; (3) Not personal expenditure; and (4) Not incurred for any illegal purpose.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical manufacturer provides luxury international vacation packages and expensive gifts to hospital doctors to incentivize prescribing its patented drugs. What is the tax treatment of these expenses?
options: Disallowed under Explanation to Section 37(1) as illegal expenses providing benefits in violation of professional conduct regulations
Allowed as legitimate sales promotion expenditure under Section 37(1)
Allowed up to 10% of total pharmaceutical turnover
Deductible under Section 35 as clinical research
questions.explanation: Under Explanation to Section 37(1), providing freebies, gifts, perquisites, or travel facilities to medical practitioners in violation of regulations governing their conduct is an illegal expenditure and is strictly disallowed.

questions.question: A corporation pays ₹10,00,000 as compounding fees to settle regulatory proceedings for statutory pollution violations. Is this expenditure deductible under Section 37(1)?
options: Deductible as an ordinary commercial settlement expense
Disallowed under Explanation to Section 37(1) as expenditure incurred to compound an offence or settle contravention proceedings (FA 2024)
Allowed provided the company upgrades its effluent treatment plant
Deductible as compensatory damages
questions.explanation: Under Explanation to Section 37(1) as amended by Finance Act 2024, any expenditure incurred to compound an offence or to settle proceedings initiated in relation to contravention of any law is strictly disallowed.

questions.question: A corporate entity incurs ₹50,00,000 on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) projects under Section 135 of the Companies Act. How is this expenditure treated under PGBP?
options: 100% deductible as an essential statutory business compliance expense
Deductible up to 2% of average net profits
Strictly disallowed under Section 37(1) because CSR is not incurred for the purpose of carrying on business
Treated as an addition to the Block of Assets
questions.explanation: Explanation 2 to Section 37(1) clarifies that any expenditure incurred by an assessee on activities relating to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) shall not be deemed to be expenditure incurred for the purpose of business or profession and is disallowed.

questions.question: An Indian company pays ₹5,00,000 for publishing an advertisement in a souvenir published by a political party. How is this treated under PGBP and Chapter VI-A?
options: Allowed as a normal advertising business deduction under Section 37(1)
Disallowed under both PGBP and Section 80GGB
Allowed as business deduction up to ₹1,00,000
Disallowed under PGBP u/s 37(2B), but eligible for 100% deduction under Section 80GGB under Chapter VI-A
questions.explanation: Under Section 37(2B), expenditure incurred on advertisements in souvenirs/brochures published by a political party is disallowed under PGBP. However, an Indian Company can claim 100% deduction for such amount as a political contribution u/s 80GGB.

questions.question: Which of the following corporate financing expenditures is ALLOWABLE as a revenue deduction under Section 37(1)?
options: Expenditure incurred on issuing bonus shares, debentures, and raising term loans
Underwriting commission and legal fees for an Initial Public Offering (IPO) of equity shares
Filing fees paid to the Registrar of Companies for increasing authorized share capital
Expenses on rights issues of equity shares
questions.explanation: Expenses incurred on IPO, FPO, Rights issues (capital expansion) and authorized capital increases are capital expenditures (disallowed). Expenses incurred on issuing bonus shares (no capital inflow), debentures, and loan borrowings are allowable revenue expenses.

questions.question: Which of the following tax payments is ALLOWABLE as a deduction under PGBP?
options: Income-tax, Surcharge, and Health & Education Cess
Goods and Services Tax (GST) paid and compensatory interest for late payment of GST (subject to Section 43B)
Interest paid for late payment of advance income-tax u/s 234B/234C
Penalty paid for breach of statutory customs regulations
questions.explanation: Direct taxes (Income-tax, Surcharge, Cess), tax interest, and statutory breach penalties are strictly disallowed. Indirect taxes (GST) and compensatory commercial interest (such as GST delay interest or contract damages) are allowable deductions.

questions.question: A cashier embezzles ₹4,00,000 of cash collections during an earlier operational year. The embezzlement is discovered during an internal audit conducted in a subsequent year. When is the business loss admissible as a deduction?
options: In the earlier period when the cash was physically misappropriated
Disallowed completely as internal management negligence
In the subsequent period in which the embezzlement is discovered
Amortized over 5 equal annual instalments
questions.explanation: Loss through employee cash embezzlement or theft is incidental to the operation of a business and is deductible under Section 37(1) in the previous year in which the embezzlement is DISCOVERED.

questions.question: A manufacturing conglomerate permanently closes down one of its five branch factories and pays retrenchment compensation of ₹18,00,000 to the retrenched workers of that unit. How is this treated?
options: Disallowed as a capital closure loss
Deductible in 10 equal instalments
Treated as an adjustment to the company's equity capital
Allowable as revenue expenditure, because retrenchment compensation on closure of individual units of an ongoing business is revenue in nature
questions.explanation: Retrenchment compensation paid on the closure of individual units/branches while the overall business continues is an allowable revenue expenditure. (Compensation paid on closure of the entire business is capital expenditure).

questions.question: A film production house spends ₹25,00,000 on producing a feature film. Due to creative disputes, the project is abandoned prior to release. How is the cost of the abandoned film treated?
options: Treated as an admissible revenue expenditure and allowed as a full deduction
Capitalized permanently without any tax write-off
Treated as a speculative loss
Allowed only if the script is sold at scrap value
questions.explanation: In the case of an abandoned film or an abandoned project relating to an existing line of business, the costs incurred are treated as revenue expenditure and allowed as a deduction in the year of abandonment.

questions.question: In Orient Ceramics and Industries Ltd, what principle was laid down by the Delhi High Court regarding dealer glow sign boards?
options: Glow sign boards represent permanent brand assets that must be capitalized to the 15% Block

Expenditure on glow sign boards displayed at dealer outlets is revenue expenditure because the boards have a short operational life, require regular replacement, and do not bring into existence any asset of enduring benefit
Signage costs are deductible only by corporate franchises
Glow sign expenses are disallowed as non-statutory advertising
questions.explanation: In Orient Ceramics and Industries Ltd, the Delhi High Court held that expenditure on glow sign boards installed at dealer premises is revenue in nature, as the assets have a short life, need frequent replacement, and do not generate an enduring capital benefit.

questions.question: A consumer electronics brand installs branded point-of-sale display counters and acrylic LED signboards across 500 retail dealerships. The AO capitalizes the ₹30,00,000 spend as a brand asset. Applying Orient Ceramics, is the AO justified?
options: Justified, because point-of-sale branding creates multi-year brand recall
Justified, unless the retail dealers pay rent for the display space
Unjustified, because point-of-sale signage and dealer display boards do not create an enduring capital asset and are deductible revenue advertising expenses
Unjustified only if the signboards are manufactured from recycled materials
questions.explanation: Applying Orient Ceramics (Delhi HC), point-of-sale display fixtures and dealer signage are sales promotion expenses that do not bring an enduring asset into existence, making the expenditure deductible as revenue expenses u/s 37(1).

questions.question: In Priya Village Roadshows Ltd., what principle did the Delhi High Court establish regarding technical feasibility and architect fees for an abandoned takeover project?
options: All feasibility expenses must be capitalized under Section 35D
Abandoned project expenses are completely non-deductible capital losses
Feasibility studies are deductible only if approved by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Feasibility studies for expanding an existing business line that are abandoned without creating a new asset are allowable as revenue expenditure
questions.explanation: In Priya Village Roadshows Ltd., the Delhi High Court held that feasibility studies and architect fees incurred for examining proposals to expand an existing business, where the venture is abandoned without creating any new asset, are allowable as revenue expenditure.

questions.question: An existing hospital operator incurs ₹8,00,000 on architect viability studies to expand its clinical wing, but drops the plan due to municipal zoning restrictions. Applying Priya Village Roadshows, what is the tax treatment?
options: Deductible as revenue expenditure u/s 37(1), because the study was conducted for the existing business line and abandoned without creating a new asset
Disallowed as an abortive capital outlay
Amortized over 5 years under Section 35D
Treated as an unabsorbed capital loss
questions.explanation: Applying Priya Village Roadshows (Delhi HC), feasibility and architectural expenses incurred for an existing business line where the venture is abandoned without creating a capital asset are deductible as revenue expenditure.

questions.question: In National Co-operative Development Corporation, what ratio was laid down by the Supreme Court regarding the relevance of the source of funding under Section 37(1)?
options: Expenditure funded from tax-exempt capital grants cannot be claimed as revenue deductions
The source of funds is irrelevant for Section 37; every application of funds towards the business objective of the assessee constitutes business expenditure, even if funded from capital receipts
Business expenses must be funded exclusively from operating cash flows
Government grants must be returned if claimed as expenses
questions.explanation: In National Co-operative Development Corporation, the Supreme Court held that the source of funds from which expenditure is made is irrelevant for Section 37. An amount may originate as a capital receipt, yet its application for business objectives remains deductible revenue expenditure.

questions.question: In Mahle Anand Filter Systems Pvt. Ltd., what principle did the Supreme Court establish regarding forgoing a capital security deposit to settle a commercial lease dispute?
options: Forgoing a capital security deposit converts it into deductible revenue expenditure if done to avoid commercial litigation
Security deposits are 100% deductible as bad debts
The underlying character of a capital security deposit does not change merely because it is forfeited to settle a dispute; it remains a non-deductible capital loss
Forfeited deposits are deductible under Section 30 as rent
questions.explanation: In Mahle Anand Filter Systems Pvt. Ltd., the Supreme Court held that forgoing a capital security deposit to end a dispute with a landlord does not convert the capital outlay into revenue expenditure. It remains capital in nature and is disallowed u/s 37(1).

questions.question: In Shanti Bhushan, what principle was established by the Delhi High Court regarding the heart surgery expenditure incurred by a professional lawyer?
options: Heart surgery is deductible as repairs to plant under Section 31
Heart surgery is deductible up to 50% under Section 37(1)
Professional medical expenses are deductible if authorized by the Bar Council
The human body/heart is not 'plant' under Section 31/43(3) and medical expenses are personal expenses without direct nexus to professional activity under Section 37(1)
questions.explanation: In Shanti Bhushan, the Delhi High Court held that the human heart is not 'plant' under Section 31/43(3). Furthermore, expenditure on heart surgery is personal in nature without direct nexus to professional efficiency, and cannot be claimed under Section 31 or Section 37(1).

questions.question: In Bank of Rajasthan Ltd. vs CIT, what principle did the Supreme Court lay down regarding 'broken-period interest' paid by banks on purchasing securities?
options: Broken-period interest paid on purchasing securities held as stock-in-trade (AFS and HFT categories) is deductible revenue expenditure; on investment securities (HTM), it is capital in nature
Broken-period interest is non-deductible across all categories
Broken-period interest is taxable as deemed banking turnover
Broken-period interest is deductible only for central government bonds
questions.explanation: In Bank of Rajasthan Ltd., the Supreme Court held that where securities are held as stock-in-trade (Available for Sale - AFS and Held for Trading - HFT), broken-period interest paid upon purchase is deductible revenue expenditure. On Held to Maturity (HTM) securities held as investments, it is capital.

questions.question: In Adadyn Technologies (P.) Ltd., what principle did the Supreme Court affirm regarding software development costs abandoned due to rapid technological obsolescence?
options: Abandoned software development costs must be capitalized to the 40% computer block

Where software development is abandoned prior to completion due to technological obsolescence without creating an enduring benefit, the expenditure incurred is deductible as revenue expenditure in the year of abandonment
Software development costs can only be claimed if transferred to an overseas entity
Disallowed as a speculative R&D loss
questions.explanation: In Adadyn Technologies (P.) Ltd., the Supreme Court affirmed that where software development expenditure is incurred but the product is abandoned due to technological obsolescence without generating any enduring benefit, the loss of outlay is deductible as revenue expenditure.

questions.question: An Indian firm pays ₹10,00,000 to a foreign consultant outside India during the previous year without deducting TDS. What is the quantum of disallowance under Section 40(a)(i)?
options: 30% of the payment (₹3,00,000)
Disallowed permanently with zero subsequent year relief
100% of the payment (₹10,00,000) is disallowed in the current previous year, and is allowable as a deduction in the previous year in which TDS is paid to the Government
Disallowed only if the consultant is an enterprise in a notified non-cooperative jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(a)(i), 100% of any sum payable/paid to a non-resident on which TDS has not been deducted or paid on or before the due date u/s 139(1) is disallowed in the current year. It is allowable in the year in which such TDS is paid.

questions.question: An assessee credits ₹5,00,000 to a resident contractor on 31st March. TDS was deducted on 31st March but was deposited with the Government after the due date of filing return of income u/s 139(1). What is the disallowance u/s 40(a)(ia)?
options: 100% of the expenditure (₹5,00,000)
No disallowance because TDS was deducted within the previous year
Disallowance of only the interest portion u/s 201(1A)
30% of the expenditure (₹1,50,000) is disallowed in the current year, and is allowable in the previous year in which the TDS is deposited
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(a)(ia), 30% of any sum paid or credited to a resident on which TDS is not deducted or not paid on or before the return filing due date u/s 139(1) is disallowed in the current PY. The 30% is allowed in the year TDS is paid.

questions.question: An assessee fails to deduct TDS on a ₹6,00,000 payment to a resident vendor. However, the vendor files its return of income, includes the receipt in total income, pays taxes, and the payer furnishes Form 26A from a CA. What is the tax result?
options: The payer is deemed to have deducted and paid TDS on the date the payee furnished its return; 30% is disallowed in the current year and allowed in the year the payee filed its return (payer liable for 1% p.m. interest u/s 201(1A))
The payer is permanently disallowed 30% of the expenditure
Full deduction is allowed in the current year without any interest penalty
The payee is penalized with a 100% penalty
questions.explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 40(a)(ia), where the payee includes the amount in its return and pays tax, and the payer furnishes Form 26A, TDS is deemed paid on the payee's return filing date. Deduction is allowed in that year, and the payer must pay 1% p.m. interest u/s 201(1A).

questions.question: In Palam Gas Service, what principle did the Supreme Court establish regarding the scope of the word 'payable' in Section 40(a)(ia)?
options: Section 40(a)(ia) applies only to amounts remaining unpaid and outstanding at the end of the previous year

The term 'payable' includes amounts actually paid during the previous year; Section 40(a)(ia) disallowance applies to sums paid during the year as well as sums payable at year-end under both cash and mercantile systems
Section 40(a)(ia) applies only to corporate assessees
Disallowance applies only if the freight contract is registered with the RTO
questions.explanation: In Palam Gas Service, the Supreme Court held that the word 'payable' in Section 40(a)(ia) includes sums actually paid during the previous year. Disallowance triggers on both amounts paid during the year and amounts remaining payable at year-end, under both cash and mercantile accounting.

questions.question: In Maruti Suzuki India Limited, what principle was established by the Delhi High Court regarding commission paid to an overseas selling agent?
options: TDS must be deducted on all foreign payments regardless of Indian chargeability
Foreign agent commission is limited to 5% of export turnover
Payments made to a non-resident agent who has no income assessable in India cannot be disallowed u/s 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of TDS merely because no nil-TDS application was made u/s 195(2)
Section 40(a)(i) applies only if the foreign agent visits India
questions.explanation: In Maruti Suzuki India Limited, the Delhi High Court held that commission paid to a foreign non-resident agent operating outside India with no taxable income in India cannot be disallowed u/s 40(a)(i) for failure to apply for a Section 195(2) nil-deduction order.

questions.question: Under Section 40(a)(iib), how is a privilege fee or royalty levied exclusively on a State Public Sector Undertaking by the State Government treated?
options: 100% deductible as an operational state licence fee
Deductible upon obtaining approval from the Finance Ministry
Treated as an advance tax credit
Strictly disallowed in the hands of the State Government undertaking
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(a)(iib), any amount paid by way of royalty, licence fee, service charge, or privilege fee which is levied exclusively on a State Government undertaking by the State Government is strictly disallowed.

questions.question: An employer pays salary to an employee outside India without deducting TDS. What is the disallowance under Section 40(a)(iii)?
options: 100% of the salary is disallowed; if TDS is not paid within the statutory due date, the salary is disallowed without subsequent-year relief
30% disallowance with subsequent year relief
Disallowed only if the employee is an Indian citizen
Treated as deemed profit of the employee
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(a)(iii), any salary payable outside India or to a non-resident on which TDS is not deducted or not paid within the prescribed time is 100% disallowed without subsequent-year cure.

questions.question: An employer provides rent-free accommodation to an employee and pays ₹80,000 tax on the non-monetary perquisite on behalf of the employee u/s 10(10CC). Can the employer claim this ₹80,000 as a business deduction?
options: Yes, as staff welfare expenditure under Section 37(1)
No, because under Section 40(a)(v), tax paid by an employer on non-monetary perquisites (which is exempt in employee hands u/s 10(10CC)) is strictly non-deductible in the employer's hands
Deductible up to ₹50,000
Yes, provided it is authorized by the board of directors
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(a)(v), any tax paid by an employer on non-monetary perquisites provided to employees (which is exempt in the hands of the employee u/s 10(10CC)) is strictly disallowed as a deduction in the hands of the employer.

questions.question: A partnership firm has a Book Profit of ₹10,00,000 before partner remuneration. What is the maximum allowable remuneration to working partners under Section 40(b)?
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(b), the maximum allowable partner remuneration is: On the first ₹3,00,000 Book Profit (or in case of loss) -> ₹1,50,000 or 90% of book profit (whichever is higher = ₹2,70,000); On the balance Book Profit (₹7,00,000) -> 60% (₹4,20,000). Maximum deduction = ₹2,70,000 + ₹4,20,000 = ₹6,90,000.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is MANDATORY for a partnership firm to claim deduction for remuneration paid to a partner u/s 40(b)?
options: The partner must be a Chartered Accountant or Advocate
The firm must be registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
The partner must not draw any capital interest
The remuneration must be paid only to a working partner, authorized by the partnership deed, relate to the period after deed execution, and fall within Section 40(b) limits
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(b), partner remuneration is deductible only if: (1) Paid to a working partner; (2) Authorized by and in accordance with the terms of the partnership deed; (3) Relates to the period after the date of the deed; and (4) Within statutory book profit limits.

questions.question: A sole proprietor purchases raw materials for ₹12,00,000 from his brother. The Fair Market Value of the raw materials is ₹9,00,000. How does the Assessing Officer deal with this transaction under Section 40A(2)?
options: Disallow the excessive and unreasonable amount of ₹3,00,000 (₹12,00,000 - ₹9,00,000) having regard to Fair Market Value
Disallow the entire payment of ₹12,00,000
No disallowance because relatives are entitled to commercial profit margins
Impose a 100% penalty on the brother
questions.explanation: Under Section 40A(2), where an assessee incurs expenditure with specified persons (relatives, partners, substantial interest holders), the AO can disallow the portion of expenditure that is excessive or unreasonable having regard to the Fair Market Value.

questions.question: What is the monetary limit under Section 40A(3) for disallowance of expenditure paid in cash to a goods transporter in a single day?
options: ₹35,000 (payment to a goods transport operator exceeding ₹35,000 in a single day otherwise than by account payee cheque/DD/ECS is disallowed)
questions.explanation: Under Section 40A(3), the general daily cash expenditure disallowance threshold is ₹10,000. However, in the case of payments made for plying, hiring, or leasing goods carriages (transporters), the daily threshold is ₹35,000.

questions.question: An assessee makes an expenditure payment of ₹45,000 by a 'Crossed Cheque' (not an Account Payee Cheque). Is this expenditure allowable under Section 40A(3)?
options: Allowable, because a crossed cheque is a banking channel instrument
Allowable up to ₹50,000
Disallowed, because Section 40A(3) strictly mandates payment by 'Account Payee Cheque', 'Account Payee DD', or specified electronic modes; a crossed cheque is treated on par with cash
Disallowed only if the cheque bounces
questions.explanation: Under Section 40A(3), payment must be made specifically by Account Payee Cheque, Account Payee Demand Draft, or ECS/prescribed electronic clearing modes. Payment by bearer cheque or crossed cheque (not account payee) is disallowed.

questions.question: An assessee claimed deduction of ₹80,000 for raw material purchases on accrual basis in Year 1. In Year 2, the assessee pays this ₹80,000 liability in cash to the supplier. What is the tax result under Section 40A(3A)?
options: The assessment of Year 1 is reopened to disallow the expenditure
₹80,000 is taxed as Short Term Capital Gain
No tax consequence because the expense was validly incurred in Year 1
The entire ₹80,000 is deemed to be profits and gains of business (PGBP income) of Year 2
questions.explanation: Under Section 40A(3A), where an expenditure was allowed on accrual basis in an earlier previous year, and subsequent payment exceeding ₹10,000 is made in cash/non-account payee mode, the payment is deemed to be PGBP income of the previous year in which payment is made.

questions.question: Which of the following cash payments exceeding ₹10,000 is PROTECTED from disallowance under Section 40A(3) by virtue of Rule 6DD?
options: Cash payment made directly to a cultivator/farmer for purchasing agricultural produce cultivated by him
Cash payment made to a retail supermarket for stationery
Cash payment made to a sub-contractor for construction labor
Cash payment made to an advertising agency
questions.explanation: Under Rule 6DD, payments made directly to primary producers/cultivators for the purchase of agricultural produce, forest produce, poultry, fish, or livestock products are exempt from Section 40A(3) cash disallowance.

questions.question: A company creates an actuarial provision of ₹10,00,000 for employee gratuity in its Profit & Loss account. No payment is made to an Approved Gratuity Fund, nor did any employee retire during the year. Is the provision deductible under Section 40A(7)?
options: 100% deductible as a scientifically computed provision

Strictly disallowed under Section 40A(7); deduction is allowed only for actual payments to an Approved Gratuity Fund or for gratuity that has become actually payable upon retirement/resignation during the PY
Deductible up to 8.33% of basic salary
Deductible in 5 equal instalments
questions.explanation: Under Section 40A(7), provisions for gratuity are disallowed. Deduction is allowed only when actual contribution is paid to an Approved Gratuity Fund (subject to Section 43B) or when gratuity actually becomes due and payable to employees during the previous year.

questions.question: Which of the following liabilities incurred during the previous year is deductible in that previous year ONLY if paid on or before the due date of filing return of income u/s 139(1)?
options: Raw material purchases from large corporate vendors
Office building rent paid to a non-relative landlord
Any tax, duty, cess, employer statutory fund contribution, employee bonus/commission, bank interest, leave encashment, and railway charges
General electricity and water utility bills
questions.explanation: Under Section 43B(a)-(g), statutory taxes, duties, cess, employee statutory fund contributions, bonus/commission, interest on loans from banks/financial institutions, leave encashment, and railway charges are deductible only if paid on or before the Section 139(1) return filing due date.

questions.question: An assessee is unable to pay outstanding bank interest of ₹6,00,000. Under a bank debt restructuring agreement, the bank converts the unpaid interest into a funded term loan. Does this conversion satisfy Section 43B actual payment?
options: Yes, because conversion into a loan legally extinguishes the interest liability
Yes, provided the term loan is repayable over a period exceeding 5 years
Yes, if approved by the Reserve Bank of India

No, under Explanations 3C & 3D to Section 43B, conversion of unpaid interest into a loan, borrowing, debenture, or deferred liability does NOT constitute actual payment; deduction is allowed only when the converted loan is actually paid off
questions.explanation: Under Explanations 3C and 3D to Section 43B, conversion of unpaid interest into a loan, borrowing, debenture, or other deferred instrument does not constitute actual payment. The interest is deductible only in the previous year in which actual payment is made.

questions.question: An assessee purchases goods from a Small Enterprise towards the end of the previous year with a written contract specifying payment within 45 days. The assessee makes payment after the expiry of the 45-day contract period in the succeeding previous year. What is the allowable timing of deduction for the purchase expenditure?
options: Allowed in the succeeding year of actual payment, because under Section 43B(h), payments to micro or small enterprises made beyond statutory limits are deductible ONLY on actual payment basis
Allowed in the year of purchase on accrual basis, provided payment was made before the statutory return filing due date
Permanently disallowed with zero deduction in any year
Apportioned 50% across both years
questions.explanation: Under Section 43B(h), any sum payable to a Micro or Small Enterprise beyond the time limit specified in Section 15 of the MSMED Act (maximum 45 days under written agreement) is deductible ONLY in the previous year of actual payment. The relaxation of paying up to the Section 139(1) return due date does NOT apply to Section 43B(h).

questions.question: An assessee purchases goods from a Micro Enterprise on 2nd March with NO written agreement regarding payment terms. Payment is made on 30th March. What is the deduction treatment under Section 43B(h)?
options: Allowed on payment basis in the next previous year

Allowed on payment basis in the current previous year (PY 1), because although payment was made after the 15-day statutory MSMED limit (17th March), it was actually paid before the close of the current previous year on 30th March
Disallowed permanently
Allowed on accrual basis
questions.explanation: Where there is no written agreement, the statutory MSMED due date is 15 days from acceptance (17th March). Since payment was made on 30th March (after 17th March), accrual deduction is lost, but because actual payment occurred within the same previous year (on 30th March), deduction is allowed on payment basis in that current previous year.

questions.question: What are the statutory investment and turnover thresholds for an entity to qualify as a 'Micro Enterprise' under the MSMED Act criteria referred in PGBP?
options: Investment in Plant & Machinery <= ₹25 Crore AND Turnover <= ₹100 Crore
Investment in Plant & Machinery <= ₹50 Lakhs AND Turnover <= ₹2 Crore
Investment in Plant & Machinery <= ₹2.5 Crore AND Turnover <= ₹10 Crore
Turnover <= ₹5 Crore with zero investment criteria
questions.explanation: Under the criteria stated in PGBP: A Micro Enterprise is an enterprise where investment in plant & machinery/equipment does not exceed ₹2.5 Crore AND turnover does not exceed ₹10 Crore. (Small Enterprise: Investment <= ₹25 Crore and Turnover <= ₹100 Crore).

questions.question: How must revenue and costs from a construction contract be recognized for tax purposes under Section 43CB and ICDS-III?
options: Completed Contract Method only upon final handover
Cash basis upon receipt of progress billing payments
Straight line amortization over 5 years
Percentage of Completion Method (POCM), where contract revenue includes retention money and contract costs are not reduced by incidental interest or dividends
questions.explanation: Under Section 43CB and ICDS-III, revenue and costs from construction contracts must be recognized under the Percentage of Completion Method (POCM). Contract revenue includes retention money, and contract costs cannot be reduced by incidental interest/dividend income.

questions.question: Under Section 43CB, what method of revenue recognition applies to a service contract with a duration of 60 days?
options: Project Completion Method, because contracts with duration up to 90 days can be recognized on project completion
Percentage of Completion Method
Straight Line Method over 12 months
Cash realization basis
questions.explanation: Under Section 43CB and ICDS-IV, for service contracts: If duration is up to 90 days -> Project Completion Method; If indeterminate acts over time -> Straight Line Method; Otherwise -> Percentage of Completion Method.

questions.question: Where a capital asset is acquired as stock-in-trade by an assessee under an amalgamation or gift, how is the Cost of Acquisition of such stock determined under Section 43C?
options: Fair Market Value on the date of amalgamation
Cost of Acquisition to the previous owner + Cost of improvement incurred by transferor/transferee + Transfer expenses incurred by transferor
NIL
Stamp Duty Value at the time of gift
questions.explanation: Under Section 43C, where a capital asset is transferred as stock-in-trade under amalgamation, gift, will, or trust, the Cost of Acquisition to the transferee is the cost of acquisition to the previous owner plus improvement costs and transfer expenses.

questions.question: Under Section 43D, when is interest income on Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) of Scheduled Banks and Public Financial Institutions chargeable to income-tax?
options: On accrual basis as per standard loan agreements
Only upon recovery of the entire principal loan amount
In the previous year in which it is credited to the Profit & Loss account by the bank OR in the previous year in which it is actually received, whichever is earlier
Exempt until the borrower is liquidated
questions.explanation: Under Section 43D, interest income on prescribed categories of bad and doubtful debts (NPAs) of banks, PFIs, SFCs, and NBFCs is chargeable to tax in the previous year in which it is credited to P&L or actually received, whichever is earlier.

questions.question: An assessee acquires machinery from an overseas supplier through a foreign currency loan. Due to exchange rate fluctuation, the rupee liability increases by ₹3,00,000. When and how is this adjustment made under Section 43A?
options: Adjusted annually on balance sheet date on marked-to-market basis
Deducted as a revenue loss under Section 37(1)
Adjusted in the Capital Reduction Reserve
Adjusted by adding ₹3,00,000 to the WDV of the Block of Assets ONLY at the time of actual payment/repayment of the foreign loan instalment
questions.explanation: Under Section 43A, exchange rate gains or losses arising on foreign currency loans taken for acquiring capital assets from abroad are adjusted to the Actual Cost / Block of Assets ONLY at the time of actual repayment of the foreign loan instalment.

questions.question: An assessee owed ₹4,00,000 for raw material purchases deducted in an earlier year. During the current year, the assessee unilaterally writes off this liability in its books without the creditor's consent. What is the tax result under Section 41(1)?
options: The unilateral write-off represents a cessation/remission of trading liability deemed to be PGBP income of the current previous year u/s 41(1)
No tax liability until the creditor provides a formal written release
Taxable under Capital Gains
Taxable under Income from Other Sources
questions.explanation: Under Section 41(1), where a trading liability was allowed as a deduction in an earlier year and the assessee unilaterally writes off the liability in accounts, it represents remission/cessation of liability deemed to be PGBP income in that previous year.

questions.question: What is the gross receipt threshold for a specified professional (e.g. Doctor, CA, Architect, IT Consultant) to compulsorily maintain Rule 6F books of account under Section 44AA?
options: Gross receipts exceeding ₹10,00,000 in any 1 preceding year
Gross receipts exceeding ₹1,50,000 in all 3 years immediately preceding the previous year (or likely to exceed in newly set-up profession)
Gross receipts exceeding ₹50,00,000 in current year
Net profit exceeding ₹2,50,000
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AA(1) and Rule 6F, specified professionals must compulsorily maintain prescribed books of account (cash book, journal, ledgers, carbon copies of bills >₹25) if gross receipts exceed ₹1,50,000 in all 3 preceding years.

questions.question: Under Section 44AB, what is the turnover threshold for compulsory tax audit for a business assessee where aggregate cash receipts and aggregate cash payments do NOT exceed 5% of total receipts/payments?
options: ₹1 Crore
₹2 Crore
₹10 Crore
₹5 Crore
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AB(a), the turnover limit for compulsory tax audit is ₹1 Crore. However, if aggregate cash receipts and cash payments during the previous year are each up to 5% of total receipts/payments, the tax audit limit is increased to ₹10 Crore.

questions.question: A resident individual engaged in retail trading has a total turnover of ₹1,80,00,000 (₹1,00,00,000 received via account payee bank transfers by return due date and ₹80,00,000 in cash). What is the minimum presumptive PGBP income u/s 44AD?
options: ₹14,40,000 (8% of entire ₹1.80 Crore)
₹10,80,000 (6% of entire ₹1.80 Crore)
₹9,00,000 (5% of entire turnover)
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AD, presumptive business income is 8% of turnover, but is reduced to 6% in respect of turnover realized by account payee cheque, DD, ECS, or digital banking channels on or before the return filing due date. Total = ₹6,00,000 + ₹6,40,000 = ₹12,40,000.

questions.question: An eligible assessee declared profits u/s 44AD for AY 24-25 and AY 25-26. In AY 26-27, he declares profits of 4% (lower than 44AD rates). What is the consequence for subsequent years?
options: He is barred from claiming the benefit of Section 44AD for the next 5 consecutive assessment years (AY 27-28 to 31-32) and must maintain books and undergo tax audit if income > basic exemption
No restriction; he can opt back into 44AD in AY 27-28
He is permanently prohibited from doing business in India
He must pay a 100% penalty on turnover
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AD(4) and (5), if an assessee declares income u/s 44AD and subsequently opts out in any of the 5 consecutive succeeding years, he is barred from 44AD for 5 consecutive AYs succeeding the opt-out year, and must maintain books and get audited u/s 44AB.

questions.question: A legal consultant (specified profession) has gross receipts of ₹48,00,000 during the previous year. What is the minimum presumptive PGBP income under Section 44ADA?
options: ₹3,84,00,000 (8% of gross receipts)
₹24,00,000 (50% of gross receipts)
₹2,88,000 (6% of gross receipts)
₹12,00,000 (25% of gross receipts)
questions.explanation: Under Section 44ADA, for an eligible resident professional with gross receipts up to ₹50 Lakhs (₹75 Lakhs if cash receipts <=5%), the presumptive PGBP income is deemed to be 50% of total gross receipts (50% of ₹48,00,000 = ₹24,00,000).

questions.question: A partnership firm opting for presumptive taxation under Section 44AD wishes to claim deductions for partner salary u/s 40(b) and interest on capital from its deemed profit. Are these deductions allowable?
options: Allowable, because partner remuneration is an essential business expense
Allowable up to ₹1,50,000

Not allowable; all deductions under Sections 30 to 38 (including partner remuneration and interest) are deemed to have been fully allowed, and cannot be deducted separately from deemed 44AD/44ADA profit
Allowable only with prior approval of the Commissioner
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AD and 44ADA, all deductions under Sections 30 to 38 are deemed to have been fully given effect to. No separate deduction for partner salary, bonus, or interest under Section 40(b) is allowable from deemed presumptive income.

questions.question: An assessee owns 2 Heavy Goods Vehicles (Gross Vehicle Weight: 16,000 kg / 16 MT each) and 3 Light Goods Vehicles throughout the 12 months of the previous year. What is the presumptive PGBP income under Section 44AE?
options: ₹4,50,000 (5 vehicles x ₹7,500 x 12 months)
₹9,60,000 (5 vehicles x 16 MT x ₹1,000 x 12 months)
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AE: For Heavy Goods Vehicles (>12 MT GVW) -> ₹1,000 per ton of GVW per month (2 x 16 x ₹1,000 x 12 = ₹3,84,000); For Other Goods Vehicles -> ₹7,500 per vehicle per month (3 x ₹7,500 x 12 = ₹2,70,000). Total presumptive income = ₹6,54,000.

questions.question: A partnership firm engaged in the transport business opts for presumptive taxation under Section 44AE. Can it claim deduction for partner salary and interest on capital under Section 40(b)?
options: Yes, unlike Section 44AD and 44ADA, partner remuneration, salary, and interest within Section 40(b) limits ARE deductible from income computed under Section 44AE
No, partner remuneration is disallowed across all presumptive schemes
Deductible only up to ₹50,000 per truck
Deductible only if the firm owns more than 10 vehicles
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AE(3), partner remuneration, salary, and interest on capital within the statutory limits of Section 40(b) ARE deductible from the deemed presumptive income computed under Section 44AE.

questions.question: What are the presumptive profit rates for Non-Residents engaged in Shipping (Section 44B) and Aircraft operations (Section 44BBA)?
options: Shipping: 10%; Aircraft: 10%
Shipping (44B): 7.5% of specified sum; Aircraft (44BBA): 5% of specified sum; lower profit declaration is not available
Shipping: 5%; Aircraft: 7.5%
Shipping: 20%; Aircraft: 15%
questions.explanation: Under Section 44B (Non-resident shipping, other than cruise ships), presumptive income is 7.5% of the specified sum. Under Section 44BBA (Non-resident aircraft operation), presumptive income is 5% of the specified sum. Option to declare lower profits is not available.

questions.question: What is the presumptive profit rate for Non-Residents providing services for mineral oil extraction (Section 44BB) and Foreign Companies executing turnkey power projects (Section 44BBB)?
options: 7.5% of specified sum without audit option
25% of specified sum
10% of the specified sum under both Section 44BB and Section 44BBB; lower profits can be claimed with books of account and Section 44AB tax audit
5% under 44BB and 15% under 44BBB
questions.explanation: Under Section 44BB (mineral oil services) and Section 44BBB (turnkey power projects), presumptive profit is 10% of the specified sum. Assessees can claim lower profits provided they maintain books u/s 44AA and undergo tax audit u/s 44AB.

questions.question: What is the presumptive profit rate under Section 44BBC for a Non-Resident operating passenger cruise ships touching Indian ports (Finance Act 2024)?
options: 7.5% of total global cruise revenue
10% of passenger tickets
5% of net vessel operating surplus
20% of the specified sum paid/payable or received/deemed received on account of carriage of passengers
questions.explanation: Under Section 44BBC (introduced by Finance Act 2024), presumptive income for a non-resident operating passenger cruise ships (meeting notification criteria: >200 passenger capacity, touching >=2 Indian ports) is 20% of the specified sum. Lower profit declaration is not available.

questions.question: How is the deduction for Head Office expenses allowable to an Indian branch of a Foreign Company computed under Section 44C?
options: Lower of 5% of Adjusted Total Income (ATI) or actual head office expenses attributable to the Indian business
100% of global head office expenses allocated on turnover ratio
10% of Indian branch gross turnover
Fixed ceiling of ₹50,00,000 per branch
questions.explanation: Under Section 44C, head office expenditure allowable to Indian branches of foreign companies is limited to the lower of: (1) 5% of Adjusted Total Income (ATI); or (2) Actual head office expenses attributable to the Indian business. If ATI is a loss, 3-year average ATI is considered.

questions.question: A non-resident entity has a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India through which it provides technical services. How is its income computed under Section 44DA?
options: Taxed at a flat gross rate without any expense deductions under Section 115A

Computed under PGBP on net basis (Sections 28 to 44D), where expenses not wholly/exclusively incurred for the PE and amounts paid by PE to Head Office (other than actual expense reimbursements) are disallowed
Exempt under double taxation avoidance treaties
Taxed on 100% gross receipts as presumptive income
questions.explanation: Under Section 44DA, royalties or FTS effectively connected with an Indian PE are computed under PGBP. Expenses not incurred wholly and exclusively for the PE and any payments made by the PE to its Head Office (except reimbursement of actual expenses) are disallowed.

questions.question: How is a 'Deficiency' (excess of member protection expenditure over general member subscriptions) treated in the assessment of a mutual trade association under Section 44A?
options: Permanently lost as mutuality disallows all losses
100% deductible against member personal income
Allowed as a deduction against other taxable income (e.g. PGBP specific services or IFOS), subject to a maximum deduction of 50% of Total Income before this deduction
Treated as an unabsorbed capital loss
questions.explanation: Under Section 44A (exception to the principle of mutuality), where a mutual trade association incurs a 'Deficiency' (member protection expenses minus general member subscriptions), such deficiency is deductible against other taxable income, subject to a maximum cap of 50% of Total Income.

questions.question: Two independent business persons jointly purchase a commercial cargo aircraft costing ₹40,00,000, contributing in a 60:40 financial ratio. Both use the aircraft for their respective separate business operations. How is depreciation claimed under Section 32?
options: Depreciation is allowed only to the party holding 60% majority ownership
The co-owners must form an AOP to claim depreciation
Depreciation is disallowed because Section 32 requires sole exclusive ownership
Depreciation is computed on the total asset value and allowed to each co-owner proportionate to their respective ownership share (60% and 40%)
questions.explanation: Under Section 32 Note 4, where an asset is jointly or partially owned by two or more assessees, depreciation is allowable to each co-owner in proportion to their respective share of ownership in the asset.

questions.question: An assessee setting up a Section 35AD specified 100-bed hospital incurs capital expenditure of ₹4,00,000 for purchasing intensive care monitors. It pays ₹3,85,000 by RTGS and ₹15,000 in cash on the same day to the medical equipment vendor. What deduction is allowable under Section 35AD?
options: ₹3,85,000, because capital expenditure payments exceeding ₹10,000 made to a person in a single day otherwise than by specified banking channels are ineligible for Section 35AD deduction
₹4,00,000, because Section 35AD allows 100% deduction on all hospital equipment
Nil, because cash payment invalidates the entire capital outlay for specified business
questions.explanation: Under Section 35AD Note 4, any capital expenditure in respect of which payment (or aggregate of payments) exceeding ₹10,000 is made to a person in a single day otherwise than by account payee cheque, DD, or ECS is ineligible for Section 35AD deduction. Hence, eligible deduction = ₹4,00,000 - ₹15,00,000 = ₹3,85,000.

questions.question: A public financial institution providing long-term infrastructure finance creates a Special Reserve. What is the maximum statutory deduction allowable under Section 36(1)(viii)?
options: Flat 20% of gross total income without any reserve ceiling

Lowest of: (1) Actual amount transferred to Special Reserve; (2) 20% of profits derived from eligible business; or (3) [200% of (Paid-up Capital + General Reserve) minus Opening balance of Special Reserve]
5% of total loan disbursements made during the previous year
100% of profits transferred to capital redemption reserve
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(viii), deduction for eligible financial corporations is the lowest of: (1) Actual transfer to Special Reserve; (2) 20% of core PGBP profits; or (3) [200% of (Paid-up Share Capital + General Reserve) minus Opening balance of Special Reserve]. Any withdrawal from the reserve is subsequently taxable u/s 41(4A).

questions.question: A cooperative society engaged in the manufacture of sugar purchases sugarcane from cane growers during the crushing season. Up to what amount is the purchase price deductible as a business expense under Section 36(1)(xvii)?
options: Actual price paid without any restriction whatsoever
Restricted to 50% of the market rate of sugar
Up to the price fixed or approved by the Government (or statutory authority) for sugarcane purchases
Disallowed completely because cooperative member transactions are mutual
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(xvii), expenditure incurred by a cooperative society engaged in the manufacture of sugar for purchase of sugarcane is allowable as a deduction up to the price fixed or approved by the Government or authority constituted under law.

questions.question: An assessee purchases goods from a Micro Enterprise towards the close of the previous year with a written agreement specifying payment within 30 days. The assessee makes payment in the immediately following month in the succeeding financial year (within the agreed 30-day window). How is the deduction timed for tax purposes?
options: Allowed in the succeeding previous year on payment basis
Disallowed completely for spilling into a new financial year
Apportioned equally across both years
Allowed in the current previous year on accrual basis, because payment was made within the contractually agreed time limit (up to 45 days) under Section 15 of MSMED Act
questions.explanation: Under Section 43B(h), if payment is made within the agreed time limit (maximum 45 days) under Section 15 of the MSMED Act, the normal mercantile accrual deduction is NOT disrupted, and the expenditure is fully allowable in Year 1 (year of purchase), even if the actual payment falls in April of Year 2.

questions.question: A partnership firm incurs a Book Loss of ₹2,50,000 before partner remuneration during the previous year. What is the maximum remuneration that can be paid and allowed as a deduction to working partners under Section 40(b)?
options: ₹1,50,000, being the statutory minimum threshold allowable on the first ₹3,00,000 of book profit or in case of book loss
Nil, because remuneration can only be paid out of positive book profits
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(b)(v), on the first ₹3,00,000 of book profit OR in case of a book loss, the maximum allowable remuneration to working partners is ₹1,50,000 or 90% of book profit, whichever is more. In case of loss, the maximum allowable deduction is ₹1,50,000.

questions.question: A partnership deed is executed on 1st October providing for interest on partner capital @12% simple interest p.a. The firm credits interest for the entire 12-month previous year. How is this interest deduction assessed for the firm?
options: Interest for the full 12 months is allowed @12% p.a.
Interest is allowed @12% p.a. ONLY for the period from 1st October to 31st March (post-deed execution); interest relating to the pre-deed period (April to September) is disallowed
The entire interest is disallowed because the deed was executed midway through the year
Allowed @6% p.a. for the full year
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(b), payment of interest to a partner is allowable only if authorized by the partnership deed and relates to the period AFTER the date of execution of the deed. Any interest relating to the period prior to the execution of the deed is strictly disallowed.

questions.question: A capital asset used in a Section 35AD specified cold chain business (cost: ₹30,00,000, 100% deduction claimed) is destroyed by fire in Year 4, and the insurer settles the claim for ₹18,00,000. How is the insurance receipt taxed?
options: Tax-free capital receipt
Taxable as Long Term Capital Gain
Taxable as PGBP business income up to the amount of deduction allowed earlier (₹18,00,000 u/s 41(1) / Section 35AD reversal)
Added to the general 15% plant block
questions.explanation: Any insurance compensation or salvage realized on an asset for which 100% deduction was allowed u/s 35AD is treated as a business receipt taxable under PGBP in the year of receipt, representing recovery/deemed profit of the deduction allowed earlier.

questions.question: A manufacturing company acquired and put to use new factory machinery on 1st November of Year 1 (claimed 10% additional depreciation in Year 1). In Year 2, the company continues manufacturing operations. How is the balance 10% additional depreciation claimed?
options: Lapses permanently because additional depreciation is an acquisition-year allowance
Added to the cost of future plant additions
Allowed only upon selling the machinery
Allowed as a deduction in Year 2 (the immediately succeeding previous year) under the third proviso to Section 32(1)(ia)
questions.explanation: Under the third proviso to Section 32(1)(ia), where an asset is put to use for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition and 50% of additional depreciation is allowed in that year, the remaining 50% (10%) is mandatorily allowed as a deduction in the immediately succeeding previous year.

questions.question: An individual carries on a retail grocery business (turnover: ₹1.2 Crore) and also practices as an interior decorator (specified profession, gross receipts: ₹30 Lakhs). Can he claim presumptive taxation under both Section 44AD and Section 44ADA concurrently?
options: Yes, he can compute business income u/s 44AD (6%/8%) for the trading business and professional income u/s 44ADA (50%) for the profession simultaneously
No, an assessee can opt for only one presumptive taxation section in a single assessment year
He must undergo mandatory tax audit for both activities
He must combine both turnovers and pay tax at a flat 50%
questions.explanation: An assessee who operates both an eligible business and an eligible specified profession can independently and simultaneously claim presumptive taxation under Section 44AD for the business and Section 44ADA for the profession, provided respective individual thresholds are satisfied.

questions.question: Under Section 33AB (Tea/Coffee/Rubber), what is the taxability of an unutilized deposit balance in NABARD upon the death of the sole proprietor or partition of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)?
options: Fully taxable as PGBP income in the hands of the legal heir / coparceners
NOT taxable as deemed income, because withdrawal upon death of the assessee or partition of an HUF is an explicit statutory exception to taxability
Taxable under Capital Gains
Taxable at a flat 30% special rate
questions.explanation: Under Section 33AB(7), unutilized deposit withdrawals are deemed PGBP income on business closure, firm dissolution, or company liquidation. However, withdrawal upon the death of an individual assessee or partition of an HUF is expressly exempt and NOT treated as deemed income.

questions.question: A biotechnology company spends ₹12,00,000 on research salaries (excluding perquisites) and ₹8,00,000 on laboratory chemicals in the 2 years prior to commencing commercial business. How are these pre-commencement research expenses treated under Section 35(1)(i)?
options: Disallowed as pre-incorporation personal expenditure
Amortized over 5 years under Section 35D

100% deductible in the previous year in which commercial business commences, because revenue expenses on salary (excluding perquisites) and materials incurred within 3 years prior to commencement are deemed incurred in the commencement year
Capitalized to the Block of Assets
questions.explanation: Under Explanation to Section 35(1)(i), revenue expenditure incurred on scientific research related to business within the 3 years immediately preceding the commencement of business (limited to salaries paid to research staff, excluding perquisites, and material expenses) is deemed to have been incurred in the previous year of business commencement and allowed as a 100% deduction in that year.

questions.question: Under Section 40A(2), what constitutes 'substantial interest' in a business or profession for triggering related-party reasonableness scrutiny?
options: Holding at least 5% equity share capital
Holding more than 51% controlling majority stake
Having a director on the board
Holding at least 20% of the voting power (in case of a company) or entitlement to at least 20% of the profits (in case of any other entity/firm) at any time during the previous year
questions.explanation: Under Explanation to Section 40A(2), a person is deemed to have a substantial interest in a business if: (1) In case of a company, the person beneficially holds shares carrying >= 20% voting power; (2) In other cases (firms/AOPs), the person is entitled to >= 20% of the profits of such concern.

questions.question: An assessee receives 3 separate invoices of ₹4,000, ₹5,000, and ₹3,500 from the same vendor on a single day and pays the aggregate sum of ₹12,500 in cash on that same day. Is this payment disallowed under Section 40A(3)?
options: Disallowed, because Section 40A(3) applies to the aggregate of payments made to a single person in a single day (₹12,500 > ₹10,000), irrespective of the number of invoices
Allowed, because each individual invoice is below the ₹10,000 threshold
Allowed up to ₹10,000 with disallowance of only the excess ₹2,500
Allowed provided the vendor issues separate receipts
questions.explanation: Section 40A(3) disallowance applies where the aggregate of payments made to a person in a single day exceeds ₹10,000 (transporters ₹35,000) otherwise than by specified banking channels. Since the aggregate daily payment is ₹12,500, the entire expenditure of ₹12,500 is disallowed.

questions.category: Power SLM Balancing Charge vs Terminal Depreciation
questions.question: A power generating undertaking on SLM owns two identical generators (Cost: ₹10,00,000 each, WDV: ₹6,00,000 each). It sells Generator 1 for ₹4,50,000 and Generator 2 for ₹12,00,000. What is the tax result?
options: Combined in Block with zero PGBP consequence
Generator 1: ₹1,50,000 Terminal Depreciation u/s 32(1)(iii) (deductible PGBP); Generator 2: ₹4,00,000 Balancing Charge u/s 41(2) (taxable PGBP) + ₹2,00,000 STCG u/s 50A
Generator 1: ₹1,50,000 STCL; Generator 2: ₹6,00,000 STCG
Generator 1: Nil; Generator 2: ₹6,00,000 Balancing Charge
questions.explanation: Under the individual asset SLM method for power units: Generator 1 (Sale ₹4.5L < WDV ₹6L) yields Terminal Depreciation of ₹1,50,000 deductible u/s 32(1)(iii). Generator 2 (Sale ₹12L > Cost ₹10L) yields Balancing Charge of ₹4,00,000 (cost minus WDV) taxable under PGBP u/s 41(2) and Capital Gain of ₹2,00,000 (sale minus cost) taxable as STCG u/s 50A.

questions.question: Which of the following books of account is specifically prescribed under Rule 6F for medical practitioners whose gross receipts exceed ₹1,50,000 in all 3 preceding years?
options: Cost audit ledger and factory output log
Electronic inventory ERP log only
Daily cash book, journal, ledger, carbon copies of machine-numbered bills exceeding ₹25, and Daily Case Register in Form No. 3C
Bank passbook and counterfoils of cheque books
questions.explanation: Under Rule 6F, specified professionals must maintain a cash book, journal, and ledger, along with carbon copies of machine-numbered bills/receipts > ₹25 and original expense vouchers. In addition, medical professionals must maintain a Daily Case Register in Form No. 3C showing patients, fees, and medicine stock.

questions.question: A business has a turnover of ₹8 Crore. During the year, cash receipts constitute 3% of total receipts, but cash payments constitute 8% of total payments. Is tax audit mandatory under Section 44AB?
options: Not mandatory, because total turnover is below the ₹10 Crore threshold
Not mandatory, because the average cash percentage is (3%+8%)/2 = 5.5%
Mandatory only if the assessee is a partnership firm

Mandatory, because to avail the ₹10 Crore threshold, BOTH cash receipts AND cash payments must each not exceed 5% of aggregate receipts/payments; since cash payments are 8% (>5%), the general ₹1 Crore threshold applies
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AB, the enhanced ₹10 Crore turnover limit applies ONLY if BOTH aggregate cash receipts AND aggregate cash payments during the previous year are each <= 5% of total receipts/payments. Since cash payments exceed 5% (8%), the higher threshold is not available, and tax audit is mandatory at ₹8 Crore turnover.

questions.category: Head Office Expenses in Loss Year
questions.question: An Indian branch of a foreign company incurs actual Head Office expenses of ₹50,00,000. In the current year, the branch's Adjusted Total Income (ATI) is a Loss of ₹20,00,000. How is the Head Office deduction computed under Section 44C?
options: 5% of the average Adjusted Total Income of the 3 immediately preceding previous years (or actual HO expenses, whichever is lower)
Nil, because 5% of a negative figure is zero
100% of actual HO expenses of ₹50,00,000
Fixed statutory deduction of ₹10,00,000
questions.explanation: Under Section 44C, head office deduction is lower of actual expenses or 5% of Adjusted Total Income (ATI). Where the ATI for the current previous year is a loss, ATI is computed as the average Adjusted Total Income of the 3 immediately preceding previous years in which there was taxable income.

questions.question: A trade association incurs member protection expenditure of ₹12,00,000 and receives general member subscriptions of ₹4,00,000, creating a Deficiency of ₹8,00,000. Its other taxable PGBP income is ₹10,00,000. What is the allowable deficiency deduction under Section 44A?
options: ₹8,00,000 in full
₹5,00,000, being restricted to a maximum of 50% of the Total Income (50% of ₹10,00,000) before this deduction
Nil, because mutuality prohibits cross-head loss set-off
questions.explanation: Under Section 44A, the deficiency (₹12,00,000 - ₹4,00,000 = ₹8,00,000) is deductible against other taxable income of the association, but the deduction is statutorily restricted to a maximum cap of 50% of the Total Income before this deduction (50% of ₹10,00,000 = ₹5,00,000).

questions.question: An assessee has PGBP profit of ₹5,00,000 before adjustments, Current Year Depreciation of ₹2,00,000, Brought Forward Business Loss of ₹4,00,000, and Unabsorbed Depreciation of ₹3,00,000. What is the taxable PGBP and unabsorbed carried forward balances?
options: Taxable PGBP: ₹1,00,000; B/f Loss Carried Forward: Nil; Unabsorbed Depreciation Carried Forward: ₹2,00,000
Taxable PGBP: Nil; All losses and depreciation absorbed
Taxable PGBP: Nil; B/f Loss Carried Forward: ₹1,00,000; Unabsorbed Depreciation Carried Forward: ₹3,00,000
Taxable PGBP: ₹3,00,000
questions.explanation: Applying the mandatory priority hierarchy u/s 32(2): Profit = ₹5,00,000. (1) Current Year Depreciation of ₹2,00,000 is deducted first -> Balance = ₹3,00,000. (2) Brought Forward Business Loss is adjusted next up to available profit -> ₹3,00,000 adjusted, leaving ₹1,00,000 B/f loss to carry forward. (3) Unabsorbed Depreciation cannot be adjusted (profit is Nil), so full ₹3,00,000 carries forward indefinitely. Taxable PGBP = Nil.

questions.question: An assessee has a loss of ₹15,00,000 from an eligible specified agricultural warehousing facility and profits of ₹20,00,000 from an eligible specified 2-star hotel business (on which the investment-linked deduction was NOT claimed). Can the warehousing loss be set off against the hotel profit?
options: No, because specified business losses can only be set off against businesses that actually claimed the investment-linked deduction
Set off is restricted to 50%
Specified losses can only be set off against identical agricultural businesses

Yes, under the statutory loss set-off rules, losses of a specified business can be set off against profits of any other specified business, whether or not the investment-linked deduction is claimed in that other business
questions.explanation: Under Section 73A, losses from any specified business referred to in Section 35AD can be set off against the profits of ANY other specified business, irrespective of whether the other specified business is claiming deduction u/s 35AD or not.

questions.question: An assessee fails to deduct TDS on a ₹10,00,000 payment to a resident sub-contractor during Year 1. In Year 2, the payee files its return, pays tax, and the payer obtains Form 26A. What is the tax result for the payer across Year 1 and Year 2?
options: Year 1: 30% (₹3,00,000) is disallowed; Year 2: ₹3,00,000 is allowed as a deduction upon furnishing Form 26A (payer remains liable for 1% p.m. interest u/s 201(1A))
30% disallowed permanently in Year 1
Year 1 assessment is revised to grant full deduction retrospectively
Payee pays 30% penalty
questions.explanation: Under Section 40(a)(ia) second proviso, 30% is disallowed in Year 1. In Year 2, upon furnishing Form 26A confirming payee return filing and tax payment, the ₹3,00,000 is allowed as a deduction in Year 2. Payer must pay 1% per month interest u/s 201(1A) up to the date of payee return filing.

questions.question: A company unable to pay ₹25,00,000 accrued loan interest to a public financial institution issues equity shares of equivalent value to the lender in full settlement of the interest liability. Does this satisfy Section 43B?
options: Yes, allotment of shares constitutes valid non-cash discharge
No, under Explanation 3C to Section 43B, conversion of interest into shares, debentures, or loan instruments does NOT constitute actual payment; deduction is allowed only upon cash redemption/payment
Yes, if approved by SEBI
Deductible as a capital loss
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 3C to Section 43B, conversion of unpaid loan interest into shares, debentures, loans, or other liability instruments does not constitute actual payment for the purposes of Section 43B.

questions.category: Depreciation Put to Use Edge Case
questions.question: A machine acquired on 15th December of Year 1 is put to use for 107 days in Year 1. On 10th May of Year 2, the machine is sold. How is depreciation allowed in Year 1 and Year 2?
options: Year 1: 50% rate; Year 2: 50% rate
Year 1: Full rate; Year 2: Pro-rata rate
Year 1: 50% of normal rate; Year 2: No depreciation allowed because the asset was sold during Year 2 and removed from the Block before year-end
Year 1: Nil; Year 2: Full rate
questions.explanation: In Year 1, since the asset was acquired and put to use for <180 days in that year, depreciation is restricted to 50% of the prescribed rate. In Year 2, upon sale of the asset, sale consideration (money payable) is deducted from the Block, and depreciation is computed on the net Closing WDV of the remaining Block (no individual asset depreciation under the Block concept).

questions.question: A tenant incurs ₹15,00,000 on constructing a permanent commercial showroom extension on leased premises. What depreciation rate applies to this 'Deemed Building' under Section 32?
options: 100% amortized over the lease term
15%, as plant and machinery
Zero depreciation because the tenant is not the legal owner of the land
10%, being the standard rate of depreciation prescribed for commercial buildings
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 1 to Section 32(1), capital expenditure on leased premises is treated as a Deemed Building owned by the tenant. It forms a building block of assets eligible for standard building depreciation (10% for commercial buildings).

questions.question: Company X sells its machinery (WDV: ₹10,00,000) to Leasing Company Y for ₹18,00,000 and immediately leases it back. What is the Actual Cost of the machinery to Lessor Y under Explanation 4A to Section 43(1)?
options: ₹10,00,000, being the WDV of the asset in the hands of Lessee X at the time of transfer
₹18,00,000, being the purchase consideration paid by Lessor Y
Fair Market Value determined by a registered valuer
NIL
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 4A to Section 43(1), in a sale and leaseback transaction, the Actual Cost of the asset to the lessor is deemed to be the Written Down Value (WDV) of the asset in the hands of the lessee at the time of transfer (₹10,00,000), preventing artificial step-up of depreciation base.

questions.question: An infrastructure company issues Zero Coupon Bonds on 20th September redeemable on 10th March of the next calendar year (tenure: 171 days). Total discount is ₹12,00,000. How many calendar months are considered for discount amortization under Section 36(1)(iiia)?
options: 6 calendar months (September has >=11 days rounded up to 1 month)
6 calendar months (September: 11 days [<15 days -> ignored]; October, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb: 5 full months; March: 10 days [<15 days -> ignored]; Total = 5 months)
171 / 30 = 5.7 months rounded to 6 months
12 months
questions.explanation: Under Section 36(1)(iiia), a fraction of a month of 15 days or more is rounded up to 1 full calendar month, and <15 days is ignored. September (11 days) is ignored (<15), March (10 days) is ignored (<15), and Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb (5 full months) make the total life 5 calendar months for amortizing the ₹12,00,000 discount.

questions.question: A corporate entity makes CSR donations of ₹10,00,000 to the PM CARES Fund and ₹5,00,000 to the Clean Ganga Fund under its statutory CSR obligations. How are these treated under PGBP and Section 80G?
options: Both are deductible under Section 37(1) as CSR business expenses
Both are allowed under Section 80G without restriction
Both are disallowed under PGBP u/s 37(1); Under Section 80G, donation to PM CARES Fund is ALLOWED, but donation to Clean Ganga Fund is STRICTLY DISALLOWED if forming part of mandatory CSR
Both are completely disallowed under all sections
questions.explanation: CSR expenses are disallowed under Section 37(1). Under Section 80G, donations to Swachh Bharat Kosh and Clean Ganga Fund are explicitly ineligible for deduction if made as part of mandatory CSR under Companies Act, whereas donations to PM CARES Fund remain eligible for Section 80G deduction.

questions.question: An eligible assessee opts out of Section 44AD in Year 3 after declaring presumptive income in Year 1 and Year 2. In Year 4, his turnover is ₹1.5 Crore and total income is ₹4,00,000 (exceeding basic exemption). What statutory compliances are mandatory for Year 4?
options: He can opt back into Section 44AD by paying a 10% surcharge
He only needs to file an affidavit with the Assessing Officer
Tax audit is not required because turnover is under ₹2 Crore
He is barred from Section 44AD for 5 consecutive years, must maintain books of account u/s 44AA, and must compulsorily get his accounts audited u/s 44AB
questions.explanation: Under Section 44AD(4) and (5), if an assessee opts out of 44AD within 5 years, he is barred from 44AD for the next 5 consecutive assessment years. Furthermore, if total income exceeds the basic exemption limit, he must maintain books u/s 44AA and compulsorily undergo tax audit u/s 44AB, even if turnover is below the normal ₹10 Crore / ₹1 Crore audit threshold.
